days.summary: Jesus meets a woman caught in sin with mercy instead of stones. Then back to Judah and Tamar, whose son ends up in the family line of Jesus.

questions.text: What connection do you find between the story of Judah and Tamar and the account given in John 8:1-11? How did Jesus treat this woman?
questions.answer: Both stories put a woman caught in sexual sin in front of men ready to execute her. Judah ordered Tamar burned (Genesis 38:24); the scribes and Pharisees wanted this woman stoned (John 8:5). In both, the accusers were guilty too. Judah was the man involved, and the men in John left “one by one” once Jesus told the sinless one to throw first (vv. 7, 9). Jesus neither shamed her nor excused her. He refused to condemn her and told her, “from now on sin no more” (v. 11).

questions.text: What do we learn about God from this passage in John? In what specific area of your life can you apply this knowledge?
questions.answer:
Jesus was the only one there without sin, so the only one with a right to throw a stone, and he chose mercy. He also didn't treat the sin as nothing; he sent her away to live differently (John 8:11). God sees through hypocrisy (vv. 6-9), deals with people one to one, and offers forgiveness before he asks for change.
To consider: Are you holding a stone over someone else, or still standing in the middle waiting to be condemned for something Jesus has already forgiven?

questions.text: What was Judah's response when he was confronted with unmistakable evidence of his sin?
questions.answer: Judah had just ordered Tamar burned (Genesis 38:24). When she sent back his signet, cord and staff, he recognized them and admitted, “She is more righteous than I,” because he had kept his son Shelah from her (v. 26). He owned it publicly and did not sleep with her again. It's the first real crack in Judah's hardness; later he offers himself as a slave in Benjamin's place (Genesis 44:33).

questions.text: What were the names of the twin sons born to Tamar? Did she ever marry the father of these children?
questions.answer: Perez and Zerah (Genesis 38:29-30). Zerah's hand came out first and the midwife tied a scarlet thread on it, but he pulled it back and Perez (the name means “breach”) was born first. Tamar never married Judah; the text says he “did not know her again” (v. 26), and it never mentions her marrying anyone after this.

questions.text: Look at Matthew 1:3. Why is Tamar's name mentioned here specifically?
questions.answer: Genealogies of the time normally traced fathers, so naming a mother was deliberate. Matthew 1:3 says Judah fathered Perez and Zerah “by Tamar,” putting the scandal right into Jesus' family tree instead of skipping it. Perez is the twin whose line runs to David (Ruth 4:18-22) and on to Jesus. Matthew seems to want readers to see that God's plan moved forward through a messy, sinful episode, and that Tamar, likely a Canaanite, had a place in it.

questions.text: What do the four women in the Matthew 1 genealogy have in common?
questions.answer:
The four are Tamar (v. 3), Rahab (v. 5), Ruth (v. 5) and “the wife of Uriah,” Bathsheba (v. 6).
• Each was a foreigner or closely tied to one: Tamar likely a Canaanite, Rahab a Canaanite of Jericho, Ruth a Moabite, Bathsheba the wife of Uriah the Hittite.
• Each story involves sexual sin or a marriage that could look improper (for Ruth, her night at Boaz's feet in Ruth 3).
• God used each one to carry the line toward David and Jesus.
Interpreters differ on Matthew's main point: Gentiles included, grace over scandal, or preparing readers for Mary's unusual pregnancy (vv. 16, 18).

questions.text: God did not choose any of the legitimate sons of Jacob to be in the line of Christ. Rather, he chose an illegitimate son, the second born of the twins, a child born of the scandals of deception, incest and prostitution to be one of the ancestors of Jesus Christ. What does this say to you about the potential of any human life?
questions.answer:
Perez came from about the worst start a family story can have, yet he became an ancestor of David and of Jesus (Matthew 1:3). No one's beginnings put them beyond God's reach or use, and no one's worth is set by how they came into the world.
To consider: Who in your life, maybe including you, has been written off because of where they came from, and how might God see them differently?

questions.text: Thinking back over the last several chapters, what effect on Jacob's family has living among the Canaanites had? Can you think of a good reason for God to move them to Egypt?
questions.answer: It has gone badly. Dinah was violated at Shechem and Simeon and Levi slaughtered the city (Genesis 34). The household had foreign gods to put away (35:2). Judah married a Canaanite woman, raised wicked sons, and slept with a woman he took for a prostitute (38). Earlier, Esau's Canaanite wives grieved Isaac and Rebekah (26:34-35). The family was being absorbed. In Egypt they would live apart in Goshen, because Egyptians wouldn't eat with Hebrews and looked down on shepherds (43:32; 46:34). There they could grow into a nation without blending in, as God had told Abraham (15:13).

quiz.q: After her accusers left, what did Jesus tell the woman?
choices: Go and offer a sacrifice at the temple
Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more
Your faith has made you well
Go and show yourself to the priest
quiz.why: Jesus refused to condemn her and told her to sin no more (John 8:11).

quiz.q: True or false: The accusers walked away one by one, starting with the youngest.
quiz.why: They left one by one, beginning with the oldest (John 8:9).

quiz.q: When Judah recognized his signet, cord and staff, what did he say about Tamar?
choices: Bring her out and let her be burned
Let her keep the things, or we'll be shamed
The LORD has judged between us
She is more righteous than I
quiz.why: Judah admitted she was more righteous because he had withheld his son Shelah from her (Genesis 38:26).

quiz.q: Which twin was born first, even though the scarlet thread was tied on his brother's hand?
quiz.why: Zerah's hand came out first, but he drew it back and Perez was born ahead of him (Genesis 38:28-30).

quiz.q: In Matthew's genealogy, which son of Judah carries the family line on toward Jesus?
quiz.why: Matthew traces the line from Judah through Perez to Hezron (Matthew 1:3).

quiz.q: True or false: In both Tamar's story and John 8, the people ready to punish the woman were guilty too.
quiz.why: Judah was the man involved with Tamar, and the men in John 8 left one by one when Jesus told the sinless one to throw first (John 8:7, 9).

quiz.q: Judah's confession was the first real crack in his hardness. How does that change show up later?
choices: He marries Tamar and raises the twins
He leaves his brothers and stays in Canaan
He offers himself as a slave in Benjamin's place
He builds an altar at Bethel
quiz.why: After admitting Tamar was more righteous than he was, Judah later offered himself as a slave in Benjamin's place (Genesis 44:33).

quiz.q: What do Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Bathsheba have in common in Matthew's genealogy?
choices: All were barren until old age
All were foreigners or closely tied to one
quiz.why: Each was a foreigner or tied to one, and God used each to carry the line toward David and Jesus (Matthew 1:3-6).

quiz.q: Why would moving to Egypt help Jacob's family, according to the study?
choices: Egypt's land was more fertile than Canaan
Egyptians kept apart from shepherds, so the family wouldn't blend in
Pharaoh promised to make them all officials
Canaan had no room left for their flocks
quiz.why: Egyptians looked down on shepherds, so the family could live apart in Goshen and grow into a nation without being absorbed (Genesis 46:34).

days.summary: Sold into Potiphar's house, Joseph refuses his master's wife, runs, and lands in prison anyway.

questions.text: Read Genesis 39. When Potiphar's wife attempted to seduce him, what did he recognize and make clear about the offense she was asking him to commit? Compare this with David's words in Psalm 51:4.
questions.answer: Joseph named two wrongs. It would betray Potiphar, who had trusted him with everything except his wife (Genesis 39:8-9). And above that, it would be sin against God: “How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?” (v. 9). David says the same after Bathsheba: “Against you, you only, have I sinned” (Psalm 51:4). Both men had wronged people, but both saw sin as first an offense against God.

questions.text: Think about some of the offenses we commonly commit against others, for example, angry words, judgmentalism, criticism, gossip, strife, divisiveness, disloyalty and selfishness. How do these sins affect our Heavenly Father?
questions.answer:
Every person is made in God's image and loved by him, so wronging them wrongs him (Genesis 9:6; James 3:9-10). Paul says bitterness, anger and slander grieve the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 4:29-31), and Jesus said what we do to the least of his people we do to him (Matthew 25:40, 45). These sins hurt the Father the way a parent is hurt when one child tears down another.
To consider: Which of these do you slip into most easily, and how would it change if you saw it as something done to God's own child?

questions.text: Make a list of the steps Joseph took in resisting temptation. Can you think of a verse that might correspond with each?
questions.answer:
• v. 8: He refused right away. James 4:7: resist the devil and he will flee from you.
• v. 9: He called it what it was, sin against God. Psalm 119:11: storing God's word in the heart keeps us from sinning against him.
• vv. 8-9: He stayed loyal to the trust he'd been given. Luke 16:10: whoever is faithful in little is faithful in much.
• v. 10: He kept saying no, day after day. Galatians 6:9: don't grow weary of doing good.
• v. 10: He wouldn't even be with her. Proverbs 5:8: keep far from her, don't go near her door.
• v. 12: When she grabbed him, he ran and left his garment behind. 1 Corinthians 6:18 and 2 Timothy 2:22: flee.
• God gave him a way out, as 1 Corinthians 10:13 promises he will.

questions.text: What did Jesus say about the subject of adultery in Matthew 5:27? What steps can we take to protect ourselves?
questions.answer:
Jesus quoted “You shall not commit adultery,” then went deeper: looking at a woman with lustful intent is already adultery in the heart (Matthew 5:27-28). His words about tearing out an eye or cutting off a hand (vv. 29-30) are widely read as deliberate overstatement: deal drastically with whatever leads you into sin.
Steps that help:
• Guard your eyes and screens, like Job's “covenant with my eyes” (Job 31:1).
• Avoid private, emotionally intimate settings with someone who isn't your spouse.
• Leave early, as Joseph did, instead of testing your strength.
• Keep investing in your marriage (Proverbs 5:15-19).
• Have a friend who can ask you hard questions.

questions.text: The crime Joseph was accused of committing was usually punishable by death. Why do you think Potiphar may have spared Joseph's life?
questions.answer: The text doesn't say, so this is inference. Verse 19 says Potiphar's anger burned but not at whom, and some think he doubted his wife's story. He may have valued Joseph too much to kill him, given how his household had prospered under him (vv. 5-6). He put him in the prison for the king's prisoners rather than executing him (v. 20). Behind it all, God was protecting Joseph for what lay ahead (v. 21; 50:20).

quiz.q: Joseph asked Potiphar's wife how he could do this great wickedness and sin against whom?
quiz.why: Joseph saw the act first as a sin against God (Genesis 39:9).

quiz.q: True or false: Potiphar's wife approached Joseph only once.
quiz.why: She spoke to him day by day, and he kept refusing her (Genesis 39:10).

quiz.q: What did Joseph leave in her hand when he ran outside?
quiz.why: She grabbed his garment, and he left it in her hand and ran (Genesis 39:12).

quiz.q: In Psalm 51:4, David says he has sinned against whom, and whom only?
quiz.why: David told God, "Against you, and you only, I have sinned" (Psalm 51:4).

quiz.q: According to Jesus, a man who looks at a woman with lust has done what?
choices: Nothing wrong until he acts on it
quiz.why: Jesus said lustful looking is adultery already committed in the heart (Matthew 5:28).

quiz.q: Besides sinning against God, what other wrong did Joseph say giving in would be?
quiz.why: Joseph would not betray Potiphar, who had trusted him with everything except his wife (Genesis 39:8-9).

quiz.q: Why do sins like gossip and angry words against others also wrong God?
choices: They break a specific temple law
Every person is made in God's image and loved by him
God only cares about sins done in public
quiz.why: People are made in God's image, so cursing or tearing them down wrongs him too (James 3:9-10).

quiz.q: What promise does the study say Joseph's escape from Potiphar's wife illustrates?
choices: God removes all temptation from the faithful
Temptation stops once you resist it the first time
God provides a way out of temptation
quiz.why: God gave Joseph a way out, as he promises to do when we are tempted (1 Corinthians 10:13).

quiz.q: True or false: Genesis 39 plainly says Potiphar spared Joseph because he doubted his wife's story.
quiz.why: The text doesn't say why; it says Potiphar's anger burned but not at whom, so any reason is inference (Genesis 39:19).

days.summary: Four Hebrew words from Genesis 38–39 to study: Judah's pledge, Tamar being “more righteous,” and Joseph's choice to “refuse” rather than “sin” against God.

questions.text: From your reading this week, choose ONE WORD to research. Is there a word that is repeated? Is there a word that strikes you as especially significant or “jumps out” at you? Is there a word that intrigues or puzzles you? Your Word of the Week:

Type in your verse reference at biblehub.com. Click the Interlinear tab (“Int” on a mobile device) at the top in order to find the word in the original language. Click the link to the Strong’s number to view the Lexical Summary. What is the Hebrew word and the Strong’s #?
What are the range of meanings you find when search the Strong’s definitions? What are synonyms or antonyms?
From the column on the right, find several other places in the Old Testament where this word is used. Click on the link to read the verse. What insight does this give you?
Now, type in your verse reference again at biblehub.com, but this time click the Commentaries tab. Browse through these to see if you can gain any additional helpful information.

What has your study taught you? Have you been able to find a point of application? As you have spent time meditating on the meaning of this word in this passage, has God given you any insight into why this word stood out to you today?
Which of God’s attributes were most clear to you this week?
questions.answer:
• Merciful: Jesus refused to condemn the woman and told her to sin no more (John 8:11).
• Holy: sin is first an offense against him (Genesis 39:9; Psalm 51:4).
• Sovereign over human mess: he carried the line of Jesus through Perez, born of Judah's sin (Matthew 1:3).
• Faithful and present: the LORD was with Joseph in Potiphar's house and again in prison (Genesis 39:2, 21).

questions.text: Which passages or insights were most meaningful to you this week? Explain.
questions.answer:
• Judah's “She is more righteous than I” (Genesis 38:26): the first time he tells the truth on himself, and the beginning of the man who later offers his life for Benjamin (Genesis 44:33).
• Joseph's “How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?” (Genesis 39:9) beside David's “Against you, you only, have I sinned” (Psalm 51:4): both saw sin as personal to God.
• John 8:1-11 read with Genesis 38: the accusers in both stories were guilty too, and the only one with the right to condemn chose mercy.

questions.text: How have you applied what you’ve discovered this week about God, others, or yourself?
questions.answer:
This week's passages press two questions: am I resisting temptation early, the way Joseph did (Genesis 39:10, 12), and am I quicker to judge others than to confess my own sin, as Judah was (Genesis 38:24)? Jesus' mercy came with a command to live differently (John 8:11).
To consider: Which step from Joseph's example (saying no right away, calling it sin, staying away, running) do you need to practice this week, and in what situation?

answers: “Pledge” appears three times in Genesis 38 (vv. 17, 18, 20), and the whole story turns on it. Judah handed over his seal, cord and staff to settle a cheap deal, and those same items exposed him three months later (Genesis 38:25).

עֵרָבוֹן (ʿērābôn), Strong's H6162. BibleHub's Strong's page spells the heading עֲרָבוֹן (erabon). In the verse it has the article: הָֽעֵרָבוֹן, “the pledge.” A noun: something handed over as security until a debt is paid.

Strong's: “a pawn (given as security),” from the root ʿārab (H6148), to exchange or become surety. Brown-Driver-Briggs: give a pledge, then receive it back once the condition is met. BibleHub's topical note adds that a pledge also identified the debtor if a dispute came up, which is exactly how Tamar used it.
Synonyms: security, collateral, guarantee, deposit, surety.
Antonyms: default, forfeit, a broken promise.
The Greek arrabōn comes from this word, and Paul uses it for the Holy Spirit as God's “guarantee” (2 Corinthians 1:22; Ephesians 1:14).

The right column lists only three verses, all in Genesis 38, so click the root ʿārab (H6148) under Word Origin.
• Genesis 38:20: Judah's friend can't find the woman to redeem the pledge.
• Genesis 43:9: Judah tells Jacob, “I will be a pledge of his safety.”
• Genesis 44:32: Judah says he became a pledge for Benjamin, then offers himself as a slave in the boy's place (v. 33).
• Isaiah 38:14: Hezekiah asks God, “be my pledge of safety!”
Insight: The man who gave up his belongings as a pledge for sin later puts up his own life as the pledge for his brother.

• Cambridge Bible: a seal and a carved staff were a chief's most personal possessions and a near-certain means of identification; Tamar's request is the turning point of the story.
• Matthew Poole: God ordered events so that Judah's sin would come to light.
• Matthew Henry: that Christ came from Judah after a chapter like this shows God chooses by grace, not merit.

Judah treated his pledge as a throwaway, and it came back to expose him. Later he offers himself as the pledge for Benjamin (Genesis 44:32-33), and God gives his Spirit as the pledge that he will finish what he began in us (Ephesians 1:13-14).
To consider: Where are you doubting that God will finish his work in you, and how does the pledge of his Spirit answer that doubt?

words.gloss: to be in the right, be just; justify
answers: Judah's confession turns on this one verb, and it's a puzzle: the woman who posed as a prostitute is the one called righteous. Working out what the word measures explains why Judah said it.
צָדַק (tsadaq), Strong's H6663. In the verse it's צָֽדְקָה (ṣā·ḏə·qāh), “she is righteous,” followed by מִמֶּנִּי, “than I.” A verb: to be right, be just, be in the right.

Strong's: “to be (causatively, make) right (in a moral or forensic sense).” Forensic means courtroom language. Brown-Driver-Briggs lists Genesis 38:26 under “have a just cause, be in the right.” Other forms mean justify, declare righteous, vindicate, acquit, do justice. It's about who has right on their side in a dispute, so it doesn't call Tamar sinless.
Synonyms: just, upright, innocent, vindicated, in the right.
Antonyms: guilty, wicked, condemned.

• Genesis 44:16: Judah again: “how can we clear ourselves? God has found out the guilt of your servants.”
• Job 9:2: “How can a man be in the right before God?”
• Psalm 51:4: David confesses so that God is “justified in your words.”
• Jeremiah 3:11: “Faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than treacherous Judah,” the same comparison, with Judah on the losing side again.
• Isaiah 53:11: God's servant will “make many to be accounted righteous.”
Insight: People can only admit someone else is more in the right than they are; God himself makes the guilty righteous.

• Cambridge Bible: the verb means to be in the right, so Judah is saying “she is in her rights as against me,” because he denied her the marriage to Shelah she was owed.
• Benson and Poole: Tamar was more at fault in the sexual sin, but Judah was more unjust, since he broke his promise and caused hers. Never going back to her showed his confession was real.
• Barnes: Judah was a harsh judge in a case where he was just as guilty.

Tamar wasn't sinless; she was in the right about what she was owed. Judah's admission is the first honest thing he says in the chapter, and the change in him starts there (Genesis 44:33).
To consider: In a conflict you're in now, have you been so focused on the other person's fault that you haven't admitted where they are in the right?

Joseph's reason for refusing Potiphar's wife comes down to this word: “sin against God.” The same verb is in David's confession, “Against you, you only, have I sinned” (Psalm 51:4), so it ties the week's two Old Testament readings together.
חָטָא (chata), Strong's H2398. In the verse it's וְחָטָאתִי (wə·ḥā·ṭā·ṯî), “and sin.” A verb: to miss, go wrong, sin.

Strong's: “properly, to miss; hence (figuratively and generally) to sin; by inference, to forfeit, lack, expiate, repent.” Brown-Driver-Briggs: “miss (a goal or way), go wrong, sin,” with Judges 20:16 for slingers who could hit a hair and not miss. In another verb form it means the opposite: to purify or cleanse from sin. It occurs about 238 times.
Synonyms: iniquity, transgression, wickedness, evil, offend, trespass.
Antonyms: righteousness, obedience; cleanse, purify.

• Genesis 20:6: God tells Abimelech, “it was I who kept you from sinning against me.”
• Genesis 42:22: Reuben: “Did I not tell you not to sin against the boy?”
• Genesis 43:9: Judah: “let me bear the blame forever,” the same verb.
• Exodus 32:30: Moses: “You have sinned a great sin.”
• Psalm 51:7: “Purge me with hyssop” uses this verb in its cleansing sense.
Insight: Sin against a person is also sin against God, and the verb that names the failure also names God's cleansing of it.

• Barnes: Joseph appealed to three things at once: honor toward a master who trusted him, chastity (“this great wickedness”), and piety (“sin against God”).
• Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: “against God” is the real principle of purity, and it is enough on its own.
• Cambridge Bible: Joseph takes the simplest line, that the act is wrong in God's sight, and the note compares Psalm 51:4.

Joseph didn't weigh the odds of getting caught; he named the act for what it was, aimed at God. Seeing sin as missing God's mark, and as personal to him, makes it more serious and also easier to confess, since the one I've wronged is the one who cleanses (Psalm 51:7).
To consider: Is there a sin you've been calling by a softer name, and what changes if you call it sin against God, as Joseph did?

“Refused” is the first thing Joseph does in the scene, before he gives a single reason (Genesis 39:8), and verse 10 shows he kept refusing day after day. It's an ordinary word, but two chapters earlier it describes Jacob refusing comfort over Joseph (Genesis 37:35), which makes it worth tracing.
מָאֵן (maʾēn), Strong's H3985. In the verse it's וַיְמָאֵן (way·mā·ʾên), “and he refused.” A verb: to refuse.

Strong's: simply “to refuse,” which the KJV sometimes renders “utterly.” Brown-Driver-Briggs: used in the intensive form and usually followed by another verb (“refused to go,” “refused to listen”); Genesis 39:8 is one of the few places it stands alone, followed by “and said.” BibleHub's topical note counts about 41 uses and describes a deliberate, accountable “No” that can be righteous resistance as well as rebellion.
Synonyms: decline, reject, withhold, resist.
Antonyms: consent, yield, comply, agree.

• Genesis 37:35: Jacob “refused to be comforted” over Joseph.
• Exodus 7:14: “Pharaoh's heart is hardened; he refuses to let the people go.”
• Deuteronomy 25:7: a brother-in-law who “refuses to perpetuate his brother's name,” the duty Onan dodged and Judah withheld (Genesis 38:9, 14).
• 2 Kings 5:16: Elisha refuses Naaman's gift.
Insight: The same word describes a hard heart refusing God and a faithful heart refusing sin; what matters is what you are saying no to.

• Matthew Henry: when trouble didn't break Joseph, Satan tried pleasure, and from someone whose favor could have advanced him; he resisted by God's grace.
• Gill: Joseph didn't just refuse but reasoned with her, naming the act as ingratitude to his master and sin against God.
• Pulpit Commentary: he answered an unclean proposal with clean words, and the note compares Psalm 51:4 for how God views the act.

Joseph said no before he explained himself, and he had to say it again every day (Genesis 39:10). The same word describes Pharaoh's no to God (Exodus 7:14); Joseph could refuse sin because he had already settled his loyalty to God.
To consider: What is one thing you need to decide ahead of time to refuse, so you aren't deciding it fresh every time it comes up?

days.summary: God was with Joseph in Potiphar's house and in prison, without changing where he was. Then a run of verses on what real prosperity and integrity look like.

questions.text: Read Genesis 39. List every phrase with verse number that describes the way in which God was with Joseph in his circumstances despite the fact that he did not change his circumstances.
questions.answer:
• v. 2: “The LORD was with Joseph”
• v. 2: he became a successful man
• v. 3: his master saw that the LORD was with him
• v. 3: the LORD caused all he did to succeed in his hands
• v. 4: Joseph found favor in Potiphar's sight
• v. 5: the LORD blessed the Egyptian's house “for Joseph's sake”
• v. 5: the LORD's blessing was on all Potiphar had, in house and field
• v. 21: “But the LORD was with Joseph”
• v. 21: he showed him steadfast love
• v. 21: he gave him favor with the keeper of the prison
• v. 22: the keeper put all the prisoners in Joseph's charge
• v. 23: “the LORD was with him”
• v. 23: whatever he did, the LORD made it succeed

questions.text: God prospered Joseph in everything he did. What do the following verses say about prosperity?
questions.answer:
• Deuteronomy 29:9: Keep and do the words of God's covenant “that you may prosper in all that you do.”
• 1 Chronicles 22:13: David tells Solomon he will prosper if he carefully obeys God's statutes; be strong and courageous, don't be afraid.
• 2 Chronicles 31:21: Hezekiah sought God in every work he took on, did it with all his heart, and prospered.
• Psalm 1:1-6: The blessed person doesn't walk in the counsel of the wicked; he delights in God's law and meditates on it day and night. He is like a tree planted by streams of water, fruitful in season, its leaf not withering, and “in all that he does, he prospers.” The wicked are like chaff; the LORD knows the way of the righteous.
• Joshua 1:1-9: Be strong and courageous, keep God's law and meditate on it day and night; then you will make your way prosperous and have good success, because the LORD is with you wherever you go (vv. 7-9).
• 3 John 2: John prays that things go well for his friend and his health is good, just as it goes well with his soul.
The common thread: prosperity grows out of obedience and a heart set on God, and God's presence is its root.

questions.text: In the original Hebrew, the word ("salah") expresses the idea of a successful venture, not merely the notion of prosperity as it pertains to the acquisition of wealth. How does this enlarge your understanding of what it means for God to prosper you?
questions.answer:
Tsalach (צָלַח) means to succeed, advance, or push through to a good end. Joseph had no money and no freedom, yet Genesis 39 uses this word for him three times (vv. 2, 3, 23): God made his work succeed in a slave's job and in a prison. So God prospering you may mean your work going somewhere good and accomplishing his purpose, whether or not your bank account changes.
To consider: In an ordinary or limited situation right now, where might God be making your work succeed in a way you haven't counted as prosperity?

questions.text: What is the meaning of the word "integrity?" In how many ways did Joseph demonstrate that he was a man of integrity in this chapter?
questions.answer:
Integrity means being whole and undivided: the same person in private as in public, with your actions matching what you believe. Joseph showed it in at least seven ways in Genesis 39:
• He served faithfully even as a slave (vv. 2-4).
• He handled everything Potiphar owned without abusing that trust (vv. 6, 8).
• He refused his master's wife out of loyalty to Potiphar (vv. 8-9).
• He cared more about sinning against God than about pleasing her (v. 9).
• He kept refusing day after day (v. 10).
• With no one else in the house, he ran rather than give in (vv. 11-12).
• He stayed faithful and responsible in prison (vv. 22-23).

questions.text: What do the following verses teach about integrity?
questions.answer:
• Psalm 41:12: God upholds the person of integrity and sets them in his presence forever.
• Psalm 25:21: David prays that “integrity and uprightness” will preserve him while he waits for God.
• Proverbs 11:3: Integrity guides the upright, but crookedness destroys the treacherous.

quiz.q: Who saw that the LORD was with Joseph and made everything he did prosper?
quiz.why: His master saw that the LORD was with him and prospered his work (Genesis 39:3).

quiz.q: Once Joseph ran his household, what was the only thing Potiphar still concerned himself with?
quiz.why: Potiphar left everything in Joseph's hand except the food he ate (Genesis 39:6).

quiz.q: What did God tell Joshua to meditate on day and night so he would prosper?
quiz.why: God told Joshua to keep the book of the law in his mouth and meditate on it, and then he would prosper (Joshua 1:8).

quiz.q: Psalm 1 says the person who delights in God's law is like what?
choices: A tree planted by streams of water
quiz.why: That person is like a tree by streams of water whose leaf doesn't wither (Psalm 1:3).

quiz.q: True or false: Proverbs says the integrity of the upright will guide them.
quiz.why: Integrity guides the upright, while the treacherous are destroyed by their crookedness (Proverbs 11:3).

quiz.q: True or false: In Genesis 39, God was with Joseph by getting him out of his hard circumstances.
quiz.why: God didn't remove Joseph's hardship; even in prison the LORD was with him and showed him steadfast love (Genesis 39:21).

quiz.q: What common thread does the study find in the verses about prosperity?
choices: Prosperity grows out of obedience and a heart set on God
Prosperity means God's people never face hardship
Prosperity comes from hard work alone
Prosperity is a reward for giving money
quiz.why: Hezekiah sought God and did every work with all his heart, and he prospered (2 Chronicles 31:21).

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew word tsalach, used of Joseph in Genesis 39, mean?
choices: To succeed or push through to a good end
quiz.why: Tsalach means to succeed or advance to a good end, and it is used of Joseph as a slave and a prisoner (Genesis 39:2-3, 23).

quiz.q: How does the study define integrity?
choices: Following every custom of your culture
Being whole and undivided, the same in private and public
quiz.why: Integrity is being the same in private as in public, as Joseph showed when he ran with no one else in the house (Genesis 39:11-12).

days.summary: Joseph in prison, and the blessing promised to Abraham spilling over onto the people around his family.

questions.text: Notice that Joseph's gifting in the area of administration was not wasted even though he was a slave in a foreign land. In a real sense, God caused Joseph to bloom where he was planted and to develop his gift in a less than ideal setting. What gifts is God using and developing in you as you wait for him in your present situation? If your first reaction is one of discouragement and the feeling that you aren't useful or being used, ask the Holy Spirit to shed his light on what he wants you to be doing. It may be that you are doing more than you think right where you are today.
questions.answer:
Joseph's gift for managing people and resources showed up in Potiphar's house and again in prison (Genesis 39:4, 22), places he never would have chosen. A waiting season can be where God quietly trains a gift rather than shelving it.
To consider: What are you already doing in your current situation, at home, at work, or with friends, that might be a gift God is growing, even if it doesn't feel significant?

questions.text: Compare Joseph's moral choices with some of those made by his brothers. How can this be of encouragement to you as a parent?
questions.answer:
His brothers chose violence and deceit. Simeon and Levi massacred Shechem (Genesis 34:25), Reuben slept with his father's concubine (35:22), the brothers plotted to kill Joseph, sold him, and lied to Jacob (37:18-33), and Judah slept with a woman he took for a prostitute (38:15-18). Joseph, raised in the same home with the same favoritism, refused sin at great cost (39:9). Children of the same parents make their own choices, and God can raise up a faithful child from a flawed household.
To consider: Where do you need to trust God with a child's choices instead of carrying them as a verdict on your parenting?

questions.text: At the end of Genesis 39, what are we told happened to Joseph in this prison?
questions.answer: Joseph was put in the prison where the king's prisoners were held (Genesis 39:20). But the LORD was with him, showed him steadfast love, and gave him favor with the keeper of the prison (v. 21). The keeper put Joseph in charge of all the prisoners and everything done there, and stopped checking on his work, because the LORD made whatever Joseph did succeed (vv. 22-23).

questions.text: Compare Genesis 39:5 with Genesis 12:2-3 and 30:27.
questions.answer: God promised Abram, “I will bless those who bless you,” and that all the families of the earth would be blessed in him (Genesis 12:2-3). Laban admitted the LORD had blessed him because of Jacob (30:27), and the LORD blessed Potiphar's house “for Joseph's sake” (39:5). The pattern repeats: outsiders who have Abraham's family in their household share in the blessing. It's an early preview of the promise reaching all nations, which the New Testament sees fulfilled in Christ (Galatians 3:8).

questions.text: How long did Joseph's period of suffering last? Compare Genesis 37:2 with 41:46.
questions.answer: About 13 years. Joseph was 17 when the events leading to his sale began (Genesis 37:2) and 30 when he stood before Pharaoh (41:46). At least two of those years came after the cupbearer forgot him (41:1). Even then, about nine more years passed, through seven years of plenty and two of famine, before he made himself known to his brothers (45:6).

quiz.q: What did Potiphar do with Joseph after hearing his wife's accusation?
choices: Put him in the prison for the king's prisoners
quiz.why: Potiphar put Joseph in the prison where the king's prisoners were held (Genesis 39:20).

quiz.q: Because the LORD was with Joseph, what did the prison keeper do?
choices: Moved him to a deeper dungeon
Put all the prisoners in Joseph's hands
quiz.why: The keeper put Joseph in charge of all the prisoners and stopped checking his work (Genesis 39:22-23).

quiz.q: Years before, who told Jacob, "The LORD has blessed me for your sake"?
quiz.why: Laban admitted the LORD had blessed him because of Jacob (Genesis 30:27).

quiz.q: True or false: The LORD blessed Potiphar's house and fields for Joseph's sake.
quiz.why: The LORD blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake, in the house and in the field (Genesis 39:5).

quiz.q: Joseph was 17 in Genesis 37 and stood before Pharaoh later. How many years passed?
quiz.why: He was seventeen at the start and thirty when he stood before Pharaoh, about thirteen years (Genesis 37:2; 41:46).

quiz.q: Using Joseph as the example, what does the study say a waiting season can be?
choices: A sign God has shelved your gifts
A place where God quietly trains a gift
Time that simply has to be endured
quiz.why: Joseph's gift for managing people and resources grew in Potiphar's house and in prison, places he never would have chosen (Genesis 39:4, 22).

quiz.q: What does Joseph's story show about children raised in the same flawed home?
choices: Each makes his own choices, and God can raise up a faithful one
The youngest is always the most faithful
Parents' sins decide their children's future
quiz.why: Raised in the same home as brothers who chose violence and deceit, Joseph refused sin at great cost (Genesis 39:9).

quiz.q: What pattern links Genesis 12:2-3, 30:27 and 39:5?
choices: Outsiders are cursed for dealing with Abraham's family
God blesses only those born in Canaan
Famine follows Abraham's family wherever it goes
Outsiders with Abraham's family in their household share the blessing
quiz.why: God promised to bless those who blessed Abram, and he blessed Potiphar's house for Joseph's sake (Genesis 39:5).

quiz.q: True or false: Joseph made himself known to his brothers soon after he stood before Pharaoh.
quiz.why: About nine more years passed, through seven years of plenty and two of famine, before he revealed himself (Genesis 45:6).

days.summary: Joseph interprets two dreams in prison and is forgotten. Paul, Hebrews and James on what suffering produces.

questions.text: Read Genesis 40. What qualities in Joseph are exemplified in each of the following verses?
questions.answer:
• vv. 6-7: Compassion and attentiveness. Though he had been wronged himself, he noticed the two officials looked troubled and asked why.
• v. 8: Humility and faith. He gave the credit to God: “Do not interpretations belong to God?”
• vv. 18-19: Honesty and courage. He told the baker the hard truth instead of softening it.

questions.text: What were the dreams of the cupbearer and the baker that Joseph interpreted? What happened to those individuals? What happened to Joseph?
questions.answer:
• The cupbearer dreamed of a vine with three branches that budded, blossomed and ripened; he pressed the grapes into Pharaoh's cup and handed it to him (Genesis 40:9-11). Joseph said that within three days Pharaoh would restore him to his post (vv. 12-13).
• The baker dreamed of three cake baskets on his head, with birds eating Pharaoh's baked goods out of the top one (vv. 16-17). Joseph said that within three days Pharaoh would hang him and birds would eat his flesh (vv. 18-19).
• On the third day, Pharaoh's birthday, the cupbearer was restored and the baker hanged, just as Joseph said (vv. 20-22).
• Joseph stayed in prison. The cupbearer forgot him (v. 23), for two whole years (41:1).

questions.text: A key theme in our study of the life of Joseph is undeserved suffering in the life of a believer. List the things that were done to Joseph that were unjust in the chapters we have read so far.
questions.answer:
• His brothers hated him and couldn't speak peacefully to him (Genesis 37:4).
• They plotted to kill him (37:18-20).
• They stripped off his robe and threw him into an empty pit (37:23-24).
• They sold him for twenty shekels of silver (37:28).
• They let their father believe he was dead (37:31-33).
• He was sold again as a slave to Potiphar (37:36; 39:1).
• Potiphar's wife pressured him daily, then falsely accused him of trying to lie with her (39:10-18).
• He was imprisoned for something he didn't do (39:20; 40:15).
• The cupbearer he had helped forgot him (40:23).

questions.text: Read 2 Corinthians 4:7-18. Write out the key phrases that are most encouraging to you. Can you apply any of these to any specific hardships you are facing now?
questions.answer:
Some phrases that stand out:
• God's treasure is carried in fragile “jars of clay” so the power is clearly his (v. 7)
• “afflicted in every way, but not crushed” (v. 8)
• “persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed” (v. 9)
• “we do not lose heart” (v. 16)
• “our inner self is being renewed day by day” (v. 16)
• this “light momentary affliction” is preparing an eternal weight of glory (v. 17)
• what is seen is temporary; what is unseen is eternal (v. 18)
To consider: What hardship are you facing right now, and which one of these phrases could you carry into it today?

questions.text: What do the Scriptures tell us about the sufferings Jesus endured?
questions.answer:
• Hebrews 2:10-11: God made Jesus, the founder of our salvation, “perfect through suffering,” and because he shares our humanity he is not ashamed to call us brothers.
• Hebrews 5:7-9: Jesus prayed with loud cries and tears; though he was the Son, “he learned obedience through what he suffered” and became the source of eternal salvation.
• Hebrews 12:2-3: For the joy set before him he endured the cross, despising its shame; thinking about the hostility he endured keeps us from growing weary.
“Perfect” here means complete, fully fitted to be our Savior, not that he had sin to correct.

questions.text: What words of instruction does the writer to the Hebrews give in Hebrews 10:32-39? What does this say to you personally in your current situation?
questions.answer:
• Remember the earlier days when you endured hard suffering after coming to faith (v. 32).
• You stood with those who were mistreated and even accepted the loss of your property joyfully, knowing you had a better, lasting possession (vv. 33-34).
• Don't throw away your confidence; it has a great reward (v. 35).
• You need endurance so that after doing God's will you receive what he promised (v. 36).
• The coming one will come soon, and the righteous live by faith (vv. 37-38).
• We are not people who shrink back, but people who have faith (v. 39).
To consider: What earlier season of God's faithfulness could you call to mind today to steady you in what you're facing now?

questions.text: What good can come of our trials according to the following verses?
questions.answer:
• Romans 5:3-5: Suffering produces endurance, endurance produces character, and character produces hope, a hope that won't put us to shame because God's love has been poured into our hearts by the Spirit.
• Matthew 5:4: Those who mourn are blessed, “for they shall be comforted.”
• Matthew 5:11-12: When we're insulted, persecuted or lied about for Jesus' sake, we can rejoice, because our reward in heaven is great and we stand with the prophets.
• James 1:2-8: Count trials as joy, because the testing of faith produces steadfastness that makes us mature and complete. If we lack wisdom in the middle of it, we ask God, who gives generously, and we ask in faith without doubting.

questions.text: Is there any trial or suffering in your life you can look back on now and be thankful for, seeing that God used it for good in your life?
questions.answer:
Joseph's suffering only made sense years later. Most of us have at least one hard season that, looking back, changed us or opened a door we would never have chosen.
To consider: What past trial can you name, and what specific good do you see from it now that you couldn't see then?

quiz.q: What did the chief cupbearer see in his dream?
quiz.why: He saw a vine with three branches whose grapes he pressed into Pharaoh's cup (Genesis 40:9-11).

quiz.q: What happened to the chief baker?
choices: He was restored to his office
He was released and sent home
He was put in charge of the prison
quiz.why: Pharaoh hanged the chief baker, just as Joseph had said (Genesis 40:22).

quiz.q: True or false: Pharaoh restored the cupbearer and hanged the baker on his birthday.
quiz.why: On the third day, Pharaoh's birthday, both dreams came true (Genesis 40:20-22).

quiz.q: Paul calls our affliction light and momentary. What does he say it produces for us?
quiz.why: Our light, brief affliction works for us an eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17).

quiz.q: In Romans 5, what is the first thing Paul says suffering produces?
quiz.why: Suffering produces perseverance, then proven character, then hope (Romans 5:3-4).

quiz.q: Joseph noticed the two officials looked troubled and asked why. What quality did that show?
quiz.why: Though he had been wronged himself, Joseph noticed their sad faces and asked what was wrong (Genesis 40:6-7).

quiz.q: What made Joseph's time in prison undeserved?
choices: He had stolen from Potiphar's house
He was punished for telling his dreams
He refused to work as a slave
He was jailed for something he didn't do
quiz.why: Potiphar's wife falsely accused him, and he was imprisoned though he had done nothing wrong (Genesis 40:15).

quiz.q: Hebrews says Jesus was made "perfect through suffering." What does "perfect" mean there?
choices: Complete, fully fitted to be our Savior
Cleansed of sin that needed correcting
Freed from ever feeling pain again
Rewarded with God's love for enduring
quiz.why: "Perfect" means complete and fully fitted to be our Savior, not that he had sin to correct (Hebrews 2:10).

quiz.q: True or false: Hebrews 10 says believers need endurance so they can receive what God promised.
quiz.why: We need endurance so that after doing God's will we receive what he promised (Hebrews 10:36).

days.summary: Joseph points to God instead of himself, asks the cupbearer to remember him, and is forgotten.

questions.text: What evidence do we have that Joseph did not grow bitter toward God despite everything that happened to him?
questions.answer: Joseph kept pointing to God instead of blaming him. In prison he said, “Do not interpretations belong to God?” (Genesis 40:8), and before Pharaoh, “It is not in me” (41:16). He kept serving faithfully, caring for the prisoners and noticing when they were sad (39:22; 40:4, 6-7). He was honest that he'd been wronged (40:15), but never accused God. Later he named his sons to credit God for helping him past his hardship and making him fruitful (41:51-52).

questions.text: See Genesis 40:8. What truth did Joseph recognize concerning our inabilities vs. God's ability? Why was he unafraid to attempt to interpret the dreams? What does this say to you about the ways in which God wants to use you?
questions.answer:
Joseph knew people can't interpret dreams on their own; the meaning belongs to God, who reveals it (Genesis 40:8; 41:16). That freed him. He wasn't counting on his own skill, so he had nothing to lose by trying, and the result was God's to give. God tends to use people who are willing to step in and then hand the credit back to him.
To consider: Is there something you've held back from because you know you can't do it, that God might be asking you to try while trusting him with the result?

questions.text: What happened when Joseph relied on man?
questions.answer: Joseph asked the cupbearer to remember him and mention him to Pharaoh, explaining that he had been stolen from his homeland and had done nothing to deserve the dungeon (Genesis 40:14-15). The cupbearer was restored and forgot him (v. 23), and Joseph sat in prison two more whole years (41:1). Readers differ on whether Joseph's request showed a lapse in trust or was simply reasonable. Either way, his release came in God's timing, not through the man's help.

questions.text: Compare Deuteronomy 6:10-12 with Genesis 40:23.
questions.answer: Deuteronomy 6:10-12 warns Israel that when God gives them cities, houses, wells and vineyards they didn't build or plant, and they eat and are full, they must take care not to forget the LORD. Genesis 40:23 shows that pattern on a small scale: once things were well with the cupbearer, he forgot Joseph. Comfort makes people forget those who helped them in hard times, and forget God most of all.

questions.text: How many ways do you see the Romans 8:28 principle at work in Joseph's life thus far?
questions.answer:
Romans 8:28 doesn't say every event is good; it says God works all things together for good for those who love him. In Joseph's life:
• His brothers' betrayal got him to Egypt (37:28, 36), which he later saw as God's doing (45:5-8; 50:20).
• Slavery in Potiphar's house trained him to manage a household and its resources (39:4-6).
• A false accusation put him in the king's prison (39:20), where Pharaoh's officials were held (40:1-3).
• Interpreting the cupbearer's dream put his name into the palace (40:9-13; 41:9-13).
• The cupbearer's forgetting meant Joseph was remembered at the moment Pharaoh needed him (41:1, 9-14).
• Years of hardship shaped a humbler man who gave God the credit (41:16).
• All of it put him in place to save Egypt and his own family from famine (41:53-57; 45:7).

questions.text: What character weakness was God working on in Joseph's life during those years between 17 and 30? What would have happened in his life if God hadn't allowed his struggles?
questions.answer: Many readers see immaturity, maybe pride: at 17 he brought a bad report about his brothers (Genesis 37:2) and told his dreams of them bowing to him to brothers who already hated him (37:5-11). Others read him as naive more than arrogant. Either way, the Joseph of chapters 40-41 is humble and gives God the credit. Without the hard years he might have stayed the pampered favorite, unready to lead, and without his place in Egypt his family could have starved in the famine (45:5-7).

questions.text: What might be a reason God is asking you to wait even though he has given you a vision for ministry?
questions.answer:
Joseph waited about 13 years between his dreams and their fulfillment; David waited years between his anointing and the throne; Moses spent 40 years in Midian (Acts 7:30). Waiting often builds the character, skill and dependence a calling needs, and God's timing involves other people and circumstances that may not be ready yet.
To consider: If God is using this wait to prepare you, what might he be shaping in you right now?

quiz.q: When the two officers said no one could interpret their dreams, what did Joseph say?
choices: My father taught me to read dreams
Only Pharaoh's magicians can do that
Wait until morning and I will tell you
quiz.why: Joseph pointed to God, asking if interpretations don't belong to him (Genesis 40:8).

quiz.q: What did Joseph ask the cupbearer to do once he was restored?
choices: Mention him to Pharaoh and get him out
Send word to his father Jacob
quiz.why: Joseph asked him to remember him and mention him to Pharaoh (Genesis 40:14).

quiz.q: True or false: Joseph admitted to the cupbearer that he deserved to be in prison.
quiz.why: Joseph said he had done nothing to deserve the dungeon (Genesis 40:15).

quiz.q: Once Israel was full in the land, what did Moses warn them to beware of?
quiz.why: Moses warned them not to forget the LORD who brought them out of Egypt (Deuteronomy 6:12).

quiz.q: Romans 8:28 says all things work together for good for whom?
choices: Those who are wise in their own eyes
Those who love God and are called by his purpose
quiz.why: The promise is for those who love God and are called according to his purpose (Romans 8:28).

quiz.q: Which of these shows Joseph didn't grow bitter toward God?
choices: He named his sons to credit God for helping him
He stopped interpreting dreams after the cupbearer forgot him
He demanded that Pharaoh punish his brothers
He refused to speak of God in Egypt
quiz.why: Joseph named his sons to credit God for helping him past his hardship and making him fruitful (Genesis 41:51-52).

quiz.q: What does the cupbearer forgetting Joseph have in common with Deuteronomy 6:10-12?
choices: Both show God punishing forgetfulness right away
Both are about keeping the Sabbath
Comfort makes people forget who helped them
quiz.why: Once things went well for him, the cupbearer forgot Joseph, the same pattern Moses warned would make Israel forget God (Genesis 40:23).

quiz.q: True or false: Romans 8:28 teaches that every event in a believer's life is good.
quiz.why: It doesn't call every event good; it says God works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28).

quiz.q: What weakness do many readers see in Joseph at 17, before his hard years?
quiz.why: He brought a bad report about his brothers and told his dreams of them bowing to brothers who already hated him (Genesis 37:2).

days.summary: Two more years in prison, then a single day takes Joseph from the dungeon to second in command of Egypt.

questions.text: Read Genesis 41. How long did Joseph remain in jail after interpreting the dream for Pharaoh's cupbearer who forgot about him? In what sense was this Joseph's darkest hour?
questions.answer: Two whole years (Genesis 41:1). It may have been his darkest hour because hope had finally seemed close. He had helped the cupbearer, asked to be remembered, and then heard nothing, after already losing about eleven years to slavery and prison. A hope raised and then dropped can hurt more than the original loss (Proverbs 13:12). The text doesn't describe Joseph's feelings, so this is a reasonable reading, not something stated.

questions.text: Compare Joseph's situation at the beginning of that day with his situation at the end of the day. What does this show us?
questions.answer: That morning Joseph was a forgotten Hebrew prisoner, hurried out of the dungeon to shave and change clothes (Genesis 41:14). By the end of the day he was second only to Pharaoh, wearing Pharaoh's signet ring, fine linen and a gold chain, riding in the second chariot while people called out “Bow the knee!” (vv. 40-43). Soon he had a new name and a wife (v. 45). When God's time comes, he can change a situation completely and quickly, and the long preparation turns out not to have been wasted.

questions.text: What example of a seed, planted long before, having remained dormant, but now bursting forth in full flower do you see in Joseph's life?
questions.answer:
• Joseph's dreams at 17, of his brothers' sheaves and then the sun, moon and stars bowing to him (Genesis 37:5-11), lay dormant for 13 years. Now Egyptians cry “Bow the knee!” before him (41:43), and soon his brothers bow too (42:6).
• His gift for interpreting dreams, first used for two prisoners (40:8-19), opens the way to Pharaoh (41:12-14).
• The skill he built running Potiphar's house and the prison (39:4, 22) now runs Egypt's food supply (41:48-49).

questions.text: Do you have any example of reaping positive results from a seed you planted long ago?
questions.answer:
Faithfulness, kindness and teaching often take years to show fruit, and the harvest usually gets noticed only in hindsight (Galatians 6:9).
To consider: What did you start years ago, a habit, a relationship, a prayer, an act of kindness, that you see bearing fruit now?

questions.text: Which seeds are you currently planting that you believe God will cause to one day grow and bear fruit?
questions.answer:
Joseph's harvest came from things he did quietly in hard places: working honestly, refusing sin, caring for others, giving God the credit. Ordinary faithfulness today is the planting.
To consider: Name one or two seeds you're planting now, in your family, friendships or work, and what you're trusting God to grow from them.

quiz.q: After the cupbearer forgot Joseph, how long passed before Pharaoh had his dreams?
quiz.why: Pharaoh dreamed at the end of two full years (Genesis 41:1).

quiz.q: When Pharaoh said he'd heard Joseph could interpret dreams, how did Joseph answer?
choices: It isn't in me; God will answer Pharaoh
Give me three days to pray
Only if you set me free first
quiz.why: Joseph said, "It isn't in me," and gave the credit to God (Genesis 41:16).

quiz.q: Which of these did Pharaoh put on Joseph when he set him over Egypt?
quiz.why: Pharaoh gave Joseph his signet ring, fine linen robes and a gold chain (Genesis 41:42).

quiz.q: True or false: Joseph named his firstborn son Ephraim.
quiz.why: His firstborn was Manasseh; Ephraim was the second son (Genesis 41:51-52).

quiz.q: What share of Egypt's produce did Joseph advise collecting during the seven good years?
quiz.why: Joseph told Pharaoh to take up a fifth of the land's produce in the plentiful years (Genesis 41:34).

quiz.q: Why might the two extra years in prison have been Joseph's darkest hour?
choices: He was moved to a harsher dungeon
Hope had seemed close, then nothing came of it
His brothers came to mock him
The keeper took away his responsibilities
quiz.why: A hope raised and then dropped can hurt more than the original loss (Proverbs 13:12).

quiz.q: Joseph went from forgotten prisoner to second only to Pharaoh in one day. What does that show?
choices: Hard work always pays off quickly
When God's time comes, he can change things completely and quickly
Joseph had been planning his release
quiz.why: That morning Joseph was rushed out of the dungeon, and by day's end he was set over all Egypt (Genesis 41:40-43).

quiz.q: Which long-dormant "seed" began to flower when Egyptians cried "Bow the knee!" before Joseph?
choices: His dreams of others bowing to him
quiz.why: His dreams at 17 of sheaves and stars bowing to him lay dormant for 13 years and began to come true (Genesis 41:43).

quiz.q: True or false: The study says the harvest from faithful seeds is often noticed only in hindsight.
quiz.why: Faithfulness and kindness often take years to show fruit, so we shouldn't grow weary of doing good (Galatians 6:9).

days.summary: Four Hebrew words from Genesis 39-40 and Psalm 25: the steadfast love God showed Joseph in prison (chesed), the remembering the cupbearer failed to do (zakar), the success God gave Joseph's work (tsalach), and the integrity David prays for while he waits (tom).

questions.text: From your reading this week, choose ONE WORD to research. Is there a word that is repeated? Is there a word that strikes you as especially significant or “jumps out” at you? Is there a word that intrigues or puzzles you? Your Word of the Week:

Type in your verse reference at biblehub.com. Click the Interlinear tab (“Int” on a mobile device) at the top in order to find the word in the original language. Click the link to the Strong’s number to view the Lexical Summary. What is the Hebrew word and the Strong’s #?
What are the range of meanings you find when search the Strong’s definitions? What are synonyms or antonyms?
From the column on the right, find several other places in the Old Testament where this word is used. Click on the link to read the verse. What insight does this give you?
Now, type in your verse reference again at biblehub.com, but this time click the Commentaries tab. Browse through these to see if you can gain any additional helpful information.

What has your study taught you? Have you been able to find a point of application? As you have spent time meditating on the meaning of this word in this passage, has God given you any insight into why this word stood out to you today?
Which of God’s attributes were most clear to you this week?
questions.answer:
• Present: the LORD was with Joseph in a slave's house and in prison (Genesis 39:2, 21).
• Loyal in love: he showed Joseph steadfast love when the people around him failed him (Genesis 39:21).
• In charge of timing: two forgotten years ended on the day Pharaoh needed an interpreter (Genesis 41:9-14).
• The one who reveals: interpretations belong to God, and he gives the answer (Genesis 40:8; 41:16).
To consider: Which of these do you most need to believe about God in your own situation this week?

questions.text: Which passages or insights were most meaningful to you this week? Explain.
questions.answer:
• Genesis 39:21: "But the LORD was with Joseph" comes right after the prison door shuts. God's steadfast love met him inside rather than getting him out.
• Genesis 40:23: One short verse holds two years of silence, and God used even the cupbearer's forgetting to bring Joseph out at the right moment.
• 2 Corinthians 4:17: Paul calls his hardships a light, momentary affliction producing eternal glory, and Joseph's thirteen years show what that looks like in a single life.
To consider: Which of these passages do you want to keep in front of you next week, and where will you put it?

questions.text: How have you applied what you’ve discovered this week about God, others, or yourself?
questions.answer:
Joseph's faithfulness showed up in small, daily choices: doing the work given to him (Genesis 39:22), refusing a private compromise (39:9), noticing two troubled faces (40:6-7), and giving God the credit (40:8).
To consider: Which one of these did you practice this week, and which one do you want to choose on purpose in the week ahead?

answers: It comes at the lowest point of Genesis 39. Joseph has just been jailed on a false charge, and the next sentence says the LORD showed him steadfast love (Genesis 39:21). Then in prison Joseph asks the cupbearer for the same thing, "do me the kindness" of remembering him (Genesis 40:14). One word, two very different givers.

חֶסֶד, chesed (KHEH-sed), Strong's H2617. On the Interlinear tab it sits under "kindness" (KJV "mercy"), with the verb "extended" in front of it: the LORD stretched out chesed to Joseph. In the verse it is spelled חָסֶד because of its position in the sentence; the dictionary form is חֶסֶד.
Gloss: loyal, faithful love; kindness; mercy.

Lexical Summary: lovingkindness, mercy, steadfast love, loyalty, faithfulness, goodness. Strong's traces it to chasad, "to be kind." Brown-Driver-Briggs counts about 247 uses and splits them into kindness people show each other (it lists Genesis 40:14 here) and God's lovingkindness, which rescues from trouble (Genesis 39:21 is listed there), keeps covenant, and is called abundant and everlasting.
• Synonyms: emet (faithfulness, truth), rachamim (compassion), chen (favor, the very next word in 39:21)
• Antonyms: cruelty (BDB sets the "man of chesed" against the cruel man in Proverbs 11:17); in the story itself, forgetting (Genesis 40:23)

• Genesis 24:27: Abraham's servant praises God for not abandoning his steadfast love and faithfulness; chesed shows up as guidance on the road.
• Genesis 32:10: Jacob says he is unworthy of the least of God's steadfast love.
• Genesis 40:14: Joseph asks the cupbearer for chesed, and the man forgets him (40:23).
• Exodus 34:6: God names himself abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness.
• Lamentations 3:22: In a destroyed Jerusalem, the LORD's steadfast love has not ended.
Insight: Chesed is God's loyalty showing up in places of loss, a road, a prison, a ruined city, and the one time Joseph looked for it from a person, it didn't come.

• Matthew Henry: Joseph was cut off from every friend and relative, but not from God; a person with a clear conscience in prison still has a good God there.
• Pulpit Commentary: the Hebrew literally says God "extended kindness" to Joseph.
• Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the jailer may have known Joseph was innocent, but a higher influence was at work.
• Keil & Delitzsch: the LORD's presence is what won Joseph the governor's trust and made his work prosper.

God's steadfast love in Genesis 39:21 didn't open the prison door; it came inside. And when Joseph asked a man for chesed, the man forgot, which puts God's loyalty and human loyalty side by side in two chapters.
To consider: Where are you waiting on someone else's kindness right now, and what would it look like to look for God's steadfast love in that same place?

words.gloss: to remember, call to mind, mention
answers: It frames Joseph's longest wait. He asks the cupbearer to remember him (Genesis 40:14), the chapter ends with "the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him" (Genesis 40:23), and two years later the same man says, "I remember my offenses today" (Genesis 41:9).

זָכַר, zakar (zaw-KAR), Strong's H2142. In Genesis 40:23 it sits under "did remember," right after "not." In 40:14 it appears twice: "remember me," and in a causative form, "make mention of me" to Pharaoh. Genesis 41:9 uses that causative form too.
Gloss: to remember, call to mind, mention.

Lexical Summary: to remember, recall, call to mind, mention. Strong's says it properly means "to mark (so as to be recognized)," and by extension to mention. Brown-Driver-Briggs describes remembering that affects present feeling, thought or action: God remembering his covenant and his people, and people remembering God's dealings or their own sins. The Topical Lexicon counts about 232 uses and notes that biblical remembering usually leads to action.
• Synonyms: make mention, think on (KJV, 40:14), be mindful
• Antonym: shakach, "forget" (H7911), the very next word in Genesis 40:23

• Genesis 8:1: God remembered Noah, and right away sent a wind to lower the waters.
• Genesis 30:22: God remembered Rachel, listened to her and opened her womb.
• Genesis 41:9: The cupbearer finally remembers, two years late, at the moment Pharaoh needs Joseph.
• Judges 16:28: Samson prays, "remember me," and asks for strength one more time.
• Psalm 25:7: David asks God not to remember his youthful sins but to remember him according to his steadfast love.
Insight: When God remembers, he acts. The cupbearer's memory failed, but its timing in 41:9 shows Joseph had not been forgotten by God.

• Benson: once the cupbearer was back at court, Joseph's kindness slipped from his mind, a picture of how the world's friendship disappoints.
• Matthew Henry: people at ease easily forget others in distress, and Joseph learned to trust God alone. Henry turns it on the reader: we blame the cupbearer, yet forget Christ, who did far more for us.
• Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the forgetting reflects no credit on the cupbearer, but God's plan required Joseph's release to come another way.
• Gill (on 40:14): asking for help wasn't a failure of faith; using lawful means while depending on God is right.

In Scripture remembering is more than recall; it moves someone to act. The cupbearer remembered Joseph only when it served Pharaoh, while every time God "remembers" in Genesis, something happens. Day Four's warning applies here too: comfort makes people forget (Deuteronomy 6:12).
To consider: Now that some hard season is behind you, what did God do in it that you could easily forget, and how could you mark it so you remember?

words.gloss: to advance, succeed, prosper; also to rush
answers: It's the most repeated key word in Genesis 39: Joseph "became a successful man" (Genesis 39:2), the LORD made all he did succeed (39:3), and again in prison (39:23). Day One introduced its meaning; a full word study shows how the rest of the Old Testament uses it, including a surprising second sense.

צָלַח, tsalach (tsaw-LAKH), Strong's H6743. In Genesis 39:2 it appears as מַצְלִיחַ (matsliach) under "successful." It is a causative form, and in 39:23 the same form has the LORD as its subject: the LORD "was making successful" whatever Joseph did.
Gloss: to advance, succeed, prosper.

Lexical Summary: to prosper, succeed, advance, thrive. Strong's: "to push forward," in many senses. Brown-Driver-Briggs lists two meanings: (1) "rush," used of the Spirit of the LORD rushing on Samson, Saul and David; (2) "advance, prosper," and in the causative "make prosperous, bring to a successful issue," with Genesis 39:3, 23 listed there. KJV renders it break out, come mightily, be profitable, prosper. About 65 uses.
• Synonym: sakal (H7919), "act wisely, have success," the word in Deuteronomy 29:9 and Joshua 1:7; Joshua 1:8 uses both
• Antonyms: fail, wither (Psalm 1:3), "not succeed" (Numbers 14:41)

• Genesis 24:21, 56: Abraham's servant watches to see whether the LORD has made his journey succeed, then says the LORD has prospered his way.
• Judges 14:6: The Spirit of the LORD rushes on Samson, the same verb.
• Psalm 1:3: The person rooted in God's word is a fruitful tree; whatever he does prospers.
• Jeremiah 12:1: Jeremiah asks why the wicked prosper; the word alone doesn't mean God approves.
• Isaiah 53:10: The LORD's will prospers in the hand of the suffering Servant.
Insight: Tsalach is a path reaching its goal by God's hand, and in Joseph and the Servant, that success comes through suffering, not around it.

• Benson: those who separated Joseph from his family couldn't take away God's presence, and that presence is what makes our work prosper. He also notes Joseph didn't try to escape but served faithfully where God put him.
• Keil & Delitzsch: "a man of prosperity" means one whom God causes to succeed in everything he undertakes, and Potiphar's trust grew as he saw it.
• Cambridge Bible: "the LORD was with Joseph" is the theme of the whole section, in trouble and success alike.

In Genesis 39 Joseph does the work, but the LORD is the one "making successful." That is why it can happen in a slave's job or a prison, without his circumstances improving first.
To consider: What work is in your hands right now that you could give to God to make succeed, measuring success by his purpose instead of by visible results?

Day One asked how Joseph showed integrity, and Psalm 25:21 asks for integrity as a guard while waiting for God. That is Joseph's situation exactly. Genesis 39 never uses the word, which makes it worth tracing elsewhere.

תֹּם, tom (rhymes with "home"), Strong's H8537. In Psalm 25:21 it's the first word of the verse, under "integrity," paired with yosher (H3476), "uprightness." Note: Proverbs 11:3, from Day One, uses a related form, tummah (H8538), which is also the word in Job 2:3.
Gloss: completeness, wholeness, integrity.

Lexical Summary: integrity, completeness, innocence, simplicity, uprightness. Strong's traces it to tamam, "to be complete, finished." Brown-Driver-Briggs lists three senses: (1) completeness, fullness; (2) innocence or simplicity, even "at random" for a soldier who drew his bow without a target (1 Kings 22:34); (3) integrity of heart or way. Its plural is the "Thummim" on the high priest's breastplate. 24 uses.
• Synonyms: yosher (uprightness), tamim (blameless), tsedeq (righteousness)
• Antonyms: crookedness, perversity, a divided or double heart (Proverbs 10:9; 11:3)

• Genesis 20:5-6: Abimelech claims integrity of heart, and God agrees; integrity starts with the heart's intent.
• 1 Kings 9:4: God tells Solomon to walk in integrity of heart and uprightness, as David did.
• Psalm 78:72: David shepherded Israel with integrity of heart and skillful hands, character and competence together, like Joseph in Potiphar's house.
• Psalm 41:12: God upholds the psalmist in his integrity and sets him in his presence.
• Proverbs 10:9: Whoever walks in integrity walks securely.
Insight: Tom means a life all of one piece, and the Old Testament keeps tying it to security. It keeps a person steady; it doesn't mean they are flawless.

• Keil & Delitzsch: tom is devotion that fills the whole person, not half-hearted or hypocritical. David wants integrity and uprightness as guards because his danger comes from his own sin as well as his enemies.
• Pulpit Commentary: David has just confessed great iniquity (v. 11), so he is probably not claiming his own integrity but asking for one he hopes to grow into by God's grace.
• Barnes: the word properly means "perfection"; he leans toward reading the verse as a plea that God would show himself upright in protecting someone who has been wronged.

In Psalm 25:21 integrity is something David asks for while he waits, not a badge he already has. Joseph's integrity looked like that: he was the same man alone with Potiphar's wife as he was in front of his master.
To consider: Where is there a gap right now between who you are in private and who you are in public, and what would wholeness look like there?

days.summary: Pharaoh's two dreams, Joseph's interpretation, and his plan to carry Egypt through the famine.

questions.text: Review Genesis 41. What similarities do you notice in the two dreams Pharaoh had?
questions.answer: Both dreams run on sevens: seven healthy cows and seven plump ears, then seven gaunt cows and seven thin ears scorched by the east wind (vv. 2–7). In each, the bad swallows up the good, and the thin cows looked no better after eating (v. 21). Both troubled Pharaoh, and none of his magicians or wise men could interpret them (v. 8). Joseph says the dream came twice because God has fixed the matter and will do it soon (v. 32).

questions.text: What qualities does Joseph demonstrate in Genesis 41:16?
questions.answer: When Pharaoh says he's heard Joseph can interpret dreams, Joseph deflects at once: “It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer” (v. 16). That shows humility (he takes no credit), honesty, and confidence in God, spoken boldly in front of the most powerful man in Egypt. There's no bitterness either, though the cupbearer had forgotten him for two whole years (40:23; 41:1).

questions.text: What is a situation you currently face in which you can echo Joseph's words: "I cannot do it, but God will"?
questions.answer:
Joseph walked into Pharaoh's court with no ability of his own to deliver what was asked, and he said so plainly. The same words fit a problem you can't fix or a person you can't change.
To consider: What are you carrying on your own strength right now that you could hand to God this morning with “I can't, but you can”?

questions.text: Joseph has learned not to take the glory that belongs to God himself. In what ways might we be tempted to "steal God's glory?"
questions.answer:
We steal God's glory whenever we accept credit for what he did. Some common ways:
• Taking praise for a gift, skill, or success without acknowledging where it came from (1 Corinthians 4:7)
• Serving or giving in order to be seen (Matthew 6:1–4)
• Telling answered-prayer stories so that we come off as the faithful one
• Assuming our planning, not God's provision, is what held things together
• False humility that fishes for compliments
Herod let the crowd call him a god and was struck down (Acts 12:21–23).

questions.text: How many times does Joseph mention the name of God in his answer to Pharaoh in vv. 25-36? What specific things does he say about God?
questions.answer:
Four times, and each one points to God as the one in charge:
• “God has revealed to Pharaoh what he is about to do” (v. 25)
• “God has shown to Pharaoh what he is about to do” (v. 28)
• The thing “is fixed by God” (v. 32)
• “God will shortly bring it about” (v. 32)
God knows the future, reveals it, decides it, and will carry it out. (Joseph also credits God in v. 16, just before this section.)

questions.text: What is the result of Joseph's boldness? What could Pharaoh clearly see about Joseph?
questions.answer: Pharaoh and his servants approved the plan (v. 37), and Pharaoh asked, “Can we find a man like this, in whom is the Spirit of God?” (v. 38). He saw that God had shown Joseph all this and that no one was as discerning and wise (v. 39). In a single day Joseph went from the dungeon to ruling over Pharaoh's house and all Egypt, second only to Pharaoh (vv. 40–41).

questions.text: Has anyone ever made that observation about your life? Has anyone ever wondered why you are so hopeful, peaceful, joyful, kind, honest or otherwise Christlike?
questions.answer:
Pharaoh, a pagan king, could see God in Joseph because Joseph kept pointing to God and his life backed up his words. People tend to notice this in ordinary moments: how someone handles waiting, unfairness, or bad news.
To consider: Who might be watching how you handle something hard right now, and what would you want them to see?

quiz.q: Who remembered Joseph and told Pharaoh about him?
quiz.why: The chief cupbearer recalled the young Hebrew who had interpreted his dream in prison (Genesis 41:9-13).

quiz.q: True or false: Joseph told Pharaoh he could interpret dreams by his own wisdom.
quiz.why: Joseph said it was not in him, but God would give Pharaoh a favorable answer (Genesis 41:16).

quiz.q: In Pharaoh's first dream, what did the seven thin cows do to the seven fat cows?
choices: They chased them into the river
They drove them out of Egypt
quiz.why: The ugly, thin cows ate up the fat ones and still looked as bad as before (Genesis 41:4, 41:20-21).

quiz.q: Why did Joseph say Pharaoh had the dream twice?
choices: Pharaoh had forgotten the first one
There would be two separate famines
The magicians had misread the first one
God had fixed the matter and would do it soon
quiz.why: Joseph said the dream was doubled because the thing was fixed by God and he would shortly bring it about (Genesis 41:32).

quiz.q: In Genesis 41:38, what did Pharaoh say was in Joseph?
quiz.why: Pharaoh asked his servants if they could find a man like this, in whom is the Spirit of God (Genesis 41:38).

quiz.q: Before Joseph was brought in, who was able to interpret Pharaoh's two dreams?
choices: No one, not even his magicians or wise men
quiz.why: Both dreams troubled Pharaoh, and none of his magicians or wise men could interpret them (Genesis 41:8).

quiz.q: What did Joseph's answer to Pharaoh in Genesis 41:16 show about him?
choices: Bitterness toward the cupbearer who forgot him
Pride in his gift for dreams
quiz.why: Joseph took no credit and boldly pointed Pharaoh to God, with no bitterness about being forgotten (Genesis 41:16).

quiz.q: True or false: The study names serving or giving in order to be seen as one way we steal God's glory.
quiz.why: Doing good to be seen by others takes credit that belongs to God (Matthew 6:1-4).

quiz.q: How many times does Joseph mention God in his answer to Pharaoh in Genesis 41:25-36?
quiz.why: Joseph names God four times: God revealed, showed, fixed, and will bring about what is coming (Genesis 41:25, 28, 32).

days.summary: Pharaoh raises Joseph up, the years of plenty arrive, and Joseph names his sons for what God has done.

questions.text: How did God give favor to Joseph in addition to the interpretations of the dreams? Why did Pharaoh elevate him?
questions.answer: Beyond the interpretation, God gave Joseph a wise, practical plan for the crisis, and Pharaoh and all his servants thought it good (v. 37). Pharaoh elevated him because he recognized “the Spirit of God” in him (v. 38) and reasoned that since God had shown Joseph all this, no one was as discerning and wise (v. 39). Joseph had told Pharaoh to find a discerning, wise man (v. 33), and Pharaoh decided Joseph was that man.

questions.text: What does God do for those who put their trust in him?
questions.answer:
• Ephesians 3:20: God is able to do far more abundantly than all we ask or think, by his power at work in us.
• Matthew 6:30: If God clothes the grass that is here today and burned tomorrow, he will much more clothe us, even when our faith is small.
• 1 Kings 3:7–15 (summarize): Solomon, feeling like “a little child,” asked for an understanding mind to govern God's people. God was pleased, gave him wisdom, and added the riches and honor he hadn't asked for, plus long life if he walked in God's ways.

questions.text: What specific points did Joseph make to Pharaoh concerning his dreams?
questions.answer:
• The two dreams are one message (vv. 25–26)
• God is showing Pharaoh what he is about to do (vv. 25, 28)
• The seven good cows and seven good ears are seven years of plenty (v. 26)
• The seven thin cows and empty ears are seven years of famine (v. 27)
• The famine will be so severe that the plenty will be forgotten (vv. 30–31)
• The dream came twice because God has fixed it and will do it soon (v. 32)

questions.text: What specific steps did Joseph commend to Pharaoh concerning how to prepare for the things God had shown him he was about to do?
questions.answer:
• Choose a discerning and wise man and set him over Egypt (v. 33)
