• Appoint overseers throughout the land (v. 34)
• Collect one-fifth of the produce during the seven good years (v. 34)
• Gather the food into the cities and store the grain under Pharaoh's authority, under guard (v. 35)
• Keep it as a reserve for the seven years of famine so the land won't perish (v. 36)

questions.text: List the things Pharaoh did for Joseph in seeking to highly exalt him. Contrast this with what his brothers did to him 13 years before.
questions.answer:
Pharaoh:
• Set him over his house and all Egypt, second only to the throne (vv. 40–41)
• Put his own signet ring on Joseph's hand (v. 42)
• Clothed him in fine linen and put a gold chain around his neck (v. 42)
• Had him ride in his second chariot while men called out “Bow the knee!” (v. 43)
• Gave him an Egyptian name, Zaphenath-paneah (v. 45)
• Gave him a wife, Asenath, daughter of the priest of On (v. 45)
His brothers stripped off his robe, threw him into an empty pit, sat down to eat while he begged, and sold him for twenty shekels of silver (37:23–28; 42:21). The stripped robe becomes royal linen, the pit becomes a chariot, and the slave becomes ruler of a nation. He was 17 then and 30 now (37:2; 41:46).

questions.text: What blessings did Joseph enjoy from Genesis 41:46-57?
questions.answer:
• Purpose: at 30 he entered Pharaoh's service and went out through all Egypt (v. 46)
• Abundance: the land produced plentifully, and he stored grain like the sand of the sea until he stopped measuring (vv. 47–49)
• A family: Asenath bore him two sons before the famine (v. 50)
• Healing: Manasseh's name says God made him forget his hardship and his father's house (v. 51)
• Fruitfulness: Ephraim's name says God made him fruitful in the land of his affliction (v. 52)
• Influence: when famine came, all Egypt and all the earth came to Joseph to buy grain (vv. 55–57)

questions.text: What were the names of Joseph's sons? What happened to them in Genesis 48:5?
questions.answer: Manasseh, the firstborn, sounds like “making to forget”: God had made him forget his hardship and his father's house (41:51). Ephraim sounds like “fruitful”: God had made him fruitful in the land of his affliction (41:52). In Genesis 48:5 Jacob claims both boys as his own sons, ranking them with Reuben and Simeon. Each became a full tribe of Israel, which gave Joseph a double portion. (Jacob then puts the younger, Ephraim, ahead in the blessing, 48:14–20.)

quiz.q: What Egyptian name did Pharaoh give Joseph?
quiz.why: Pharaoh called Joseph Zaphenath-paneah and gave him Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, as his wife (Genesis 41:45).

quiz.q: How old was Joseph when he entered Pharaoh's service?
quiz.why: Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh king of Egypt (Genesis 41:46).

quiz.q: Why did Joseph name his firstborn son Manasseh?
choices: God had made him forget his hardship and his father's house
God had made him fruitful in the land of his affliction
God had heard his cry from the pit
God had given him favor with Pharaoh
quiz.why: Joseph said God had made him forget all his hardship and his father's house; the fruitful name was Ephraim (Genesis 41:51-52).

quiz.q: Ephesians 3:20 says God is able to do far more abundantly than what?
choices: All that we ask or think
quiz.why: God is able to do far more abundantly than all we ask or think, by his power at work in us (Ephesians 3:20).

quiz.q: True or false: In Genesis 48:5, Jacob claims Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons, like Reuben and Simeon.
quiz.why: Jacob told Joseph that his two sons born in Egypt were now his, just as Reuben and Simeon were (Genesis 48:5).

quiz.q: In 1 Kings 3, what did Solomon ask God for?
choices: An understanding mind to govern God's people
quiz.why: Solomon asked for an understanding mind, and God added the riches and honor he hadn't asked for (1 Kings 3:7-15).

quiz.q: True or false: Joseph told Pharaoh his two dreams carried two separate messages.
quiz.why: Joseph said the two dreams were one message about what God was about to do (Genesis 41:25-26).

quiz.q: How much of the produce did Joseph advise collecting during the seven good years?
quiz.why: Joseph told Pharaoh to appoint overseers and take one-fifth of the produce during the plentiful years (Genesis 41:34).

quiz.q: Pharaoh's gifts reversed what the brothers did. What replaced the robe they stripped from Joseph?
choices: A new coat of many colors
quiz.why: Pharaoh clothed Joseph in fine linen and put a gold chain around his neck (Genesis 41:42).

days.summary: Famine drives the brothers to Egypt, where they bow to a brother they don't recognize. Joseph tests them.

questions.text: Read Genesis 42-44. What situation caused the ten brothers to make the three-week journey to Egypt?
questions.answer: A severe famine struck Canaan along with all the surrounding lands (41:57; 42:5). Jacob heard there was grain in Egypt, asked his sons why they stood looking at one another, and sent them to buy grain so the family would live and not die (42:1–2). Ten of them went (v. 3).

questions.text: Why didn't Jacob allow Benjamin (a grown man by this time) to go with them?
questions.answer: Jacob feared “harm might happen to him” (42:4). Benjamin was Rachel's only remaining son and Joseph's full brother, and as far as Jacob knew, Joseph was dead. He wasn't going to risk losing the last one. It also shows Jacob still favored Rachel's sons, and perhaps that he didn't fully trust the ten with Benjamin.

questions.text: Assuming Joseph was motivated by love and not revenge, try to think of his reason for each of the following actions:
items: Speaking harshly to his brothers and accusing them of being spies
Binding Simeon and taking him as a prisoner until they would return
Putting the silver back in their sacks
Putting the silver cup in Benjamin's sack
questions.answer:
• Speaking harshly to his brothers and accusing them of being spies (42:7–14): to hide who he was and test whether the men who had lied about him were now honest
• Imprisoning them for three days (42:17): to give them a small taste of the pit and prison he had known, and time to think
• Binding Simeon and taking him as a prisoner until they would return (42:24): to make sure they came back, and to see whether they would abandon another brother. Reuben, the eldest, had tried to save Joseph (42:22), so the next eldest was held
• Requiring Benjamin's return (42:20): to see his full brother alive and learn how they treated Rachel's other son
• Putting the silver back in their sacks (42:25): a gift of free food for his family, and a test of honesty; they did bring it back (43:12, 21)
• Giving Benjamin 5 times as much (43:34): to see whether they still resented a favored brother the way they had resented him
• Putting the silver cup in Benjamin's sack (44:2): the final test, whether they would let Benjamin become a slave to save themselves, as they once sold Joseph

questions.text: How does Genesis 42:21 show us that Joseph was beginning to get the results he desired?
questions.answer: Not knowing Joseph understood them, the brothers said, “In truth we are guilty concerning our brother” (42:21). They remembered his distress and pleading and tied their present trouble to that sin. Reuben added that a reckoning for his blood had come (v. 22). Joseph wanted their consciences awake and honest, and here they were, more than twenty years later, confessing. He turned away and wept (v. 24).

questions.text: From Genesis 42:28, why did the brothers blame God?
questions.answer: When one brother found his silver back in his sack, their hearts failed, and they turned trembling to one another: “What is this that God has done to us?” (42:28). Guilt colored how they read everything. Already convinced they were being paid back for Joseph (v. 21), they took an unexplained gift as God setting them up for punishment, and they feared being accused of theft.

questions.text: What role did a guilty conscience play in the lives of these brothers?
questions.answer: Their guilt never went away. It surfaced more than twenty years later at the first sign of trouble (42:21–22). It made them assume God was against them (42:28; 44:16), filled them with fear, and kept the old wound open between them, with Reuben still saying “I told you so.” It also made them honest, and Joseph used it to bring them to confession and real change. Even after Jacob died, they still feared Joseph would pay them back (50:15).

questions.text: What role does the emotion of guilt play in your life? Do you act based on feelings of guilt? Do you try to motivate others by means of guilt?
questions.answer:
Guilt can lead somewhere good, as it eventually did for the brothers, or it can run quietly in the background and steer choices. Using it on children, a spouse, or friends can get results without changing anyone's heart.
To consider: Think of one decision from this week. Did you make it because it was right, or because you'd have felt guilty otherwise?

quiz.q: How many of Joseph's brothers went down to Egypt the first time to buy grain?
quiz.why: Ten brothers went, because Jacob kept Benjamin home for fear harm would come to him (Genesis 42:3-4).

quiz.q: What did Joseph accuse his brothers of being?
quiz.why: Remembering his dreams, Joseph told them they were spies who had come to see the land's weakness (Genesis 42:9).

quiz.q: Which brother did Joseph bind and keep in Egypt?
quiz.why: Joseph took Simeon from among them and bound him before their eyes (Genesis 42:24).

quiz.q: True or false: In Genesis 42:21, the brothers admitted they were guilty for ignoring their brother's pleading.
quiz.why: They told one another they were guilty concerning their brother, whose distress they saw but would not hear (Genesis 42:21).

quiz.q: At Joseph's meal, how much bigger was Benjamin's portion than his brothers'?
quiz.why: Benjamin's portion was five times as much as any of theirs (Genesis 43:34).

quiz.q: Why was Benjamin so precious to Jacob that he wouldn't send him to Egypt?
choices: He had been sick as a child
He was Rachel's only remaining son
quiz.why: With Joseph presumed dead, Benjamin was Rachel's last son, and Jacob feared harm might come to him (Genesis 42:4).

quiz.q: According to the study, what was Joseph testing by hiding his silver cup in Benjamin's sack?
choices: Whether they'd abandon Benjamin to save themselves
Whether his steward could be trusted
Whether they could pay for more grain
quiz.why: The cup was the final test of whether they would let Benjamin become a slave to save themselves, as they once sold Joseph (Genesis 44:2).

quiz.q: Why did the brothers think God was against them when they found their silver returned?
choices: Joseph told them God was angry
Jacob had warned them before they left
Guilt over Joseph colored how they read everything
quiz.why: Already sure they were being paid back for Joseph, they read an unexplained gift as God setting them up (Genesis 42:28).

quiz.q: True or false: Even after Jacob died, the brothers still feared Joseph would pay them back.
quiz.why: Their guilt never fully went away; after Jacob's death they feared Joseph would repay them for the evil they did (Genesis 50:15).

days.summary: What Scripture says about guilt: seared consciences, cleansing through Christ, and no condemnation.

questions.text: Does the absence of feelings of guilt mean no fault or sin is involved? What can happen to our consciences? See 1 Timothy 4:2.
questions.answer: No. A person can do wrong and feel nothing. Paul warns that some will depart from the faith, following deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through liars whose consciences are “seared” (1 Timothy 4:1–2), burned numb like cauterized skin. Repeatedly ignoring the conscience dulls it. Feelings aren't the final measure of right and wrong; God's Word is.

questions.text: Does a feeling of guilt necessarily mean sin is involved? Is there such a thing as false guilt? Can you think of an example?
questions.answer: No. Guilt feelings can come from real sin, but also from a conscience shaped by family rules, other people's expectations, or the accuser (Revelation 12:10). Examples of false guilt: feeling guilty for saying no when you truly don't have the capacity, for a grown child's choices you couldn't control, for resting, or for a sin already confessed and forgiven. Paul also describes a “weak” conscience that condemns what God permits (Romans 14; 1 Corinthians 8). His counsel is not to override it but to let Scripture inform it over time (Romans 14:23).

questions.text: How can you distinguish between false guilty feelings (condemnation) and the conviction of the Holy Spirit?
questions.answer:
Conviction from the Holy Spirit (John 16:8) is specific. It names a particular sin, points you to Christ, and leads to confession and repentance. Once you confess, it lifts, and relief and peace follow (1 John 1:9). Paul says godly grief “produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret” (2 Corinthians 7:10).
Condemnation is vague and global: “you're a failure,” “God is tired of you.” It attacks who you are rather than what you did, keeps accusing after you've confessed, and pushes you away from God instead of toward him.
A quick test: Is there something specific to confess? If so, confess it. If you already have, the accusing voice isn't God's (Romans 8:1, 33–34).

questions.text: Why does Jesus desire to cleanse our consciences? See Hebrews 9:14-15. Why is this so important?
questions.answer: The blood of Christ, who offered himself without blemish through the eternal Spirit, will “purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Hebrews 9:14). As mediator of the new covenant, his death redeems us from our transgressions so we can receive the promised eternal inheritance (v. 15). This matters because a guilty conscience keeps us at a distance from God and stuck trying to earn our way back. A cleansed one frees us to serve him out of gratitude rather than fear.

questions.text: What is the answer to the problem of guilt in the life of a Christian? See Romans 3:21-23.
questions.answer: The answer is a righteousness that comes from God, not from us: “the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe” (v. 22). It has been revealed apart from the law (v. 21). There's no distinction between people, because all have sinned and fall short of God's glory (v. 23). Guilt isn't solved by trying harder or feeling worse, but by trusting Christ, through whom we are justified by grace as a gift (v. 24).

questions.text: What promise is made to you in Romans 8:1? What is the condition?
questions.answer: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). The promise is that no verdict of condemnation stands against you, and it's true now, not someday. The condition is being “in Christ Jesus,” united to him by faith. (The KJV adds “who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit” to this verse; most modern translations, including the ESV, follow manuscripts that have that phrase only in v. 4.)

questions.text: What help does 1 John 3:11-24 give us in dealing with a guilty conscience?
questions.answer:
• Loving others in action is evidence that we belong to God (vv. 14, 18–19); loving “in deed and in truth” reassures our hearts before him
• When our heart condemns us, “God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything” (v. 20). Our feelings aren't the final judge; he is
• When our heart doesn't condemn us, we have confidence before God and freedom in prayer (vv. 21–22)
• His command is simple: believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another (v. 23)
• The Spirit he has given us assures us that he abides in us (v. 24)

quiz.q: In 1 Timothy 4:2, what has happened to the consciences of the liars Paul describes?
quiz.why: Paul says these liars have consciences that are seared, branded as with a hot iron (1 Timothy 4:2).

quiz.q: According to Hebrews 9:14, what purifies our conscience from dead works?
quiz.why: The blood of Christ, who offered himself without blemish to God, purifies our conscience to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14).

quiz.q: True or false: Romans 3:21 says God's righteousness has been revealed through keeping the law.
quiz.why: God's righteousness has been revealed apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ (Romans 3:21-22).

quiz.q: Who does Romans 8:1 say face no condemnation?
choices: Those who do more good than bad
Those who are in Christ Jesus
quiz.why: There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1).

quiz.q: What does 1 John 3:20 say when our heart condemns us?
choices: God is greater than our heart
quiz.why: If our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything (1 John 3:20).

quiz.q: What does it mean that some people have a "seared" conscience?
choices: It is extra sensitive to sin
It has been burned numb and no longer warns them
It has been cleansed by grace
It belongs to a brand-new believer
quiz.why: A seared conscience is burned numb like cauterized skin, so a person can do wrong and feel nothing (1 Timothy 4:1-2).

quiz.q: True or false: The study says a feeling of guilt always means sin is involved.
quiz.why: Guilt feelings can come from real sin, but also from false sources such as the accuser (Revelation 12:10).

quiz.q: How does the study describe the Holy Spirit's conviction?
choices: Vague, telling you you're a failure
It keeps accusing after you confess
It pushes you away from God
Specific, pointing you to Christ and confession
quiz.why: The Spirit's conviction names a particular sin and leads to confession, then lifts once you confess (John 16:8).

quiz.q: According to the study, when is Romans 8:1's promise of no condemnation true for those in Christ?
quiz.why: There is "now" no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus; no verdict stands against them today (Romans 8:1).

days.summary: Judah, who once sold his brother, offers himself in Benjamin's place.

questions.text: What role did Judah play in this part of the story? What evidence of growth and change do you see in him?
questions.answer: Judah is the spokesman. When the cup is found, he leads the brothers back to Joseph's house, falls before him, and admits “God has found out the guilt of your servants” (44:14–16). He pleads at length, describing their father's love for Benjamin, says Jacob's life “is bound up in the boy's life” (v. 30), and offers to stay as a slave in Benjamin's place (v. 33). Growth: the man who once proposed selling Joseph for profit (37:26–27) now offers himself for Rachel's other son, speaks of his father's favoritism without resentment, and can't bear to watch his father's grief (v. 34).

questions.text: What do you think was the turning point in Judah's life?
questions.answer: Many point to Genesis 38. After losing two sons of his own (38:7–10), Judah was publicly exposed by Tamar and admitted, “She is more righteous than I” (38:26), the first time we see him own his sin. Burying two sons may also have taught him what Jacob felt over Joseph. Years of watching his father grieve, and pledging himself as surety for Benjamin (43:8–9), likely deepened the change.

questions.text: How many times are we told Joseph wept? What was the cause for each specific time?
questions.answer:
Eight times (seven, if you count 45:14–15 as one scene):
• 42:24: He hears his brothers confess their guilt over him and Reuben's rebuke; he turns away and weeps
• 43:30: He sees Benjamin, his mother's son, and has to leave the room to weep in private
• 45:2: He reveals himself to his brothers and weeps so loudly that the Egyptians and Pharaoh's household hear
• 45:14: He falls on Benjamin's neck and weeps
• 45:15: He kisses all his brothers and weeps on them
• 46:29: He meets Jacob in Goshen after more than twenty years and weeps on his neck a good while
• 50:1: Jacob dies; Joseph falls on his father's face and weeps over him
• 50:17: His brothers, afraid after Jacob's death, send a message asking forgiveness; he weeps when they speak

questions.text: How would you characterize Jacob's words and feelings in Genesis 42:36? Was he wrong? What can this show us about ourselves?
questions.answer:
Jacob says, “All this has come against me” (42:36), blaming his sons for bereaving him: Joseph gone, Simeon gone, and now they want Benjamin. It's grief mixed with self-pity and despair. The grief was real, but his conclusion was wrong. Joseph and Simeon were both alive, and everything was working toward saving his family (50:20). We do the same when we judge God's purposes from inside the hard moment.
To consider: Where are you reading “against me” into something God may be using for good?

questions.text: Do you believe the brothers repented for their actions towards their brother Joseph and father Jacob? What evidence do you see?
questions.answer:
Yes, the evidence points that way:
• They confessed their guilt among themselves (42:21) and before Joseph (44:16)
• They brought the returned silver back instead of keeping it (43:12, 21)
• When the cup was found, they tore their clothes and all went back with Benjamin rather than leaving him (44:13)
• Judah offered himself as a slave in Benjamin's place (44:33)
• They showed real concern for their father's grief (44:30–34)
• After Jacob's death they asked Joseph's forgiveness and offered themselves as his servants (50:17–18)
Scripture never records them confessing to Jacob, so that part is an inference. And fear was still mixed in with their repentance (50:15).

quiz.q: Which brother spoke for the others when they were brought back to Joseph's house?
quiz.why: Judah and his brothers fell before Joseph, and Judah answered for them all (Genesis 44:14-16).

quiz.q: After the cup was found, what did Judah say God had done?
choices: Hidden the cup to test them
Found out the guilt of his servants
quiz.why: Judah said God had found out the guilt of your servants (Genesis 44:16).

quiz.q: Judah told Joseph their father's life was bound up in whose life?
quiz.why: Judah said Jacob's life was bound up in the boy's life, and he would die without Benjamin (Genesis 44:30-31).

quiz.q: True or false: Judah asked that Benjamin stay as a slave so the rest could go home.
quiz.why: Judah asked to stay as Joseph's slave in Benjamin's place and let the boy go home (Genesis 44:33).

quiz.q: In Genesis 42:36, how did Jacob describe everything that was happening?
choices: It is all for my good
It is a test from God
All this has come against me
quiz.why: Jacob said Joseph and Simeon were gone, they wanted Benjamin, and all this had come against him (Genesis 42:36).

quiz.q: Years before offering himself for Benjamin, what had Judah proposed doing with Joseph?
quiz.why: Judah once proposed selling Joseph for profit, which makes his offer to take Benjamin's place a real change (Genesis 37:26-27).

quiz.q: Many point to which event as the turning point in Judah's life?
choices: Being held in an Egyptian prison
Being exposed by Tamar in Genesis 38
quiz.why: Exposed by Tamar, Judah admitted she was more righteous than he, the first time we see him own his sin (Genesis 38:26).

quiz.q: Why did Joseph leave the room to weep in Genesis 43:30?
choices: He heard that Jacob was ill
He saw Benjamin, his mother's son
His brothers bowed down to him
quiz.why: Seeing Benjamin, his mother's son, moved Joseph so deeply that he went out to weep in private (Genesis 43:30).

quiz.q: True or false: When the cup was found, all the brothers went back to the city with Benjamin.
quiz.why: They tore their clothes and all returned with Benjamin rather than leaving him, a sign of real repentance (Genesis 44:13).

days.summary: Four words to study from Genesis 41–43: rûaḥ “Spirit” (Pharaoh sees God's Spirit in Joseph), bîn “discerning” (shared with Solomon in 1 Kings 3), ʾāšēm “guilty” (the brothers' confession), and ʿārab “pledge” (Judah stands surety for Benjamin).

questions.text: From your reading this week, choose ONE WORD to research. Is there a word that is repeated? Is there a word that strikes you as especially significant or “jumps out” at you? Is there a word that intrigues or puzzles you? Your Word of the Week:

Type in your verse reference at biblehub.com. Click the Interlinear tab (“Int” on a mobile device) at the top in order to find the word in the original language. Click the link to the Strong’s number to view the Lexical Summary. What is the Hebrew word and the Strong’s #?
What are the range of meanings you find when search the Strong’s definitions? What are synonyms or antonyms?
From the column on the right, find several other places in the Old Testament where this word is used. Click on the link to read the verse. What insight does this give you?
Now, type in your verse reference again at biblehub.com, but this time click the Commentaries tab. Browse through these to see if you can gain any additional helpful information.

What has your study taught you? Have you been able to find a point of application? As you have spent time meditating on the meaning of this word in this passage, has God given you any insight into why this word stood out to you today?
Which of God’s attributes were most clear to you this week?
questions.answer:
• God knows and governs the future: he showed Pharaoh what he was about to do and had fixed it (Genesis 41:25, 32)
• God gives more than we ask: Solomon asked for wisdom and received riches and honor too (1 Kings 3:13; Ephesians 3:20)
• God sees hidden sin: “God has found out the guilt of your servants” (Genesis 44:16)
• God cleanses and does not condemn those in Christ (Hebrews 9:14; Romans 8:1)
To consider: Which of these is hardest for you to believe right now?

questions.text: Which passages or insights were most meaningful to you this week? Explain.
questions.answer:
• Genesis 42:21: more than twenty years later, the brothers name their guilt to each other, and Joseph turns away to weep. Their consciences had never let it go.
• Genesis 44:33: Judah, who proposed selling Joseph, asks to be a slave in Benjamin's place, the clearest picture in Genesis of a changed heart.
• Romans 8:1 with 2 Corinthians 7:10: conviction names a specific sin and leads to repentance and relief; condemnation stays vague and keeps accusing.
To consider: Which of these do you want to remember the next time guilt shows up?

questions.text: How have you applied what you’ve discovered this week about God, others, or yourself?
questions.answer:
This week's application is honesty before God: name real sin specifically, confess it, and then stop paying for what Christ has already covered (1 John 1:9; Romans 8:1). Judah adds a second step. A changed heart takes responsibility for others (Genesis 44:33).
To consider: What one specific thing did God bring to mind this week, and what have you done about it?

answers: Pharaoh, who worshiped other gods, looked at Joseph and saw “the Spirit of God” in him (Genesis 41:38). The same word shows up earlier in the chapter, when Pharaoh's own spirit was troubled by his dreams (Genesis 41:8). A troubled spirit and God's Spirit in one chapter make it worth tracing.

Hebrew: רוּחַ (rûaḥ), Strong's H7307. In the interlinear it sits under “the Spirit” in the phrase rûaḥ ʾĕlōhîm, “the Spirit of God.”
Gloss: spirit, wind, breath.

Strong's gives a wide range: wind, breath, life, mind, temper or courage, and spirit, including the Spirit of God. The NASB translates it “wind” 98 times, “breath” 31 times, and “spirit/Spirit” over 200 times. Context decides, and sometimes the overlap is the point: the breath that gives life and the Spirit who gives life share one word.
• Related: nᵉšāmâ, “breath” (H5397), paired with rûaḥ in Genesis 7:22
• Contrast: bāśār, “flesh” (H1320), human frailty set against God's Spirit (Genesis 6:3)

• Genesis 1:2: the Spirit of God hovering over the waters at creation
• Genesis 41:8: Pharaoh's spirit is troubled; he has power but no answer
• Genesis 45:27: Jacob's spirit revives when he hears Joseph is alive
• Numbers 27:18: Joshua is chosen as “a man in whom is the Spirit,” almost Pharaoh's exact phrase
• Exodus 31:3: Bezalel is filled with the Spirit of God for skill and understanding
Insight: In the Old Testament the Spirit equips particular people for particular work, and Joseph is the first person in the Bible described as having the Spirit of God in him.

• Ellicott: Pharaoh came to see Joseph as the instrument God had spoken through, and noticed that the interpretation came with wise, practical counsel.
• Keil & Delitzsch: “the Spirit of Elohim” here means a spirit of supernatural insight and wisdom.
• Cambridge Bible: Belshazzar says nearly the same thing about Daniel (Daniel 5:14); in the Old Testament the Spirit explains wisdom or strength beyond ordinary human capacity (Exodus 31:3; Numbers 27:18).

Pharaoh saw the Spirit in Joseph through how he handled a crisis: humble about the source (Genesis 41:16), clear about the facts, practical about what to do next. God's presence showed up as wisdom and honesty in front of someone who didn't share Joseph's faith.
To consider: What would someone who doesn't know God see in the way you handle the next problem you can't solve on your own?

“Discerning and wise” appears twice within a few verses: Joseph tells Pharaoh to find such a man (Genesis 41:33), and Pharaoh decides no one fits it like Joseph (Genesis 41:39). The same pair turns up in this week's cross-reference, when God gives Solomon “a wise and discerning mind” (1 Kings 3:12).

Hebrew: נָבוֹן (nāḇôn), a participle of the verb בִּין (bîn), Strong's H995. In the interlinear it sits under “discerning” in both Genesis 41:33 and 41:39, right beside חָכָם (ḥāḵām, “wise,” H2450).
Gloss: to discern, understand, distinguish.

Strong's says the root idea is “to separate mentally,” to tell one thing from another. From there it covers perceive, consider, pay attention, understand, be prudent, and teach. The NASB uses “understand” most often, then “discern/discerning.” The emphasis is less on cleverness than on seeing what is really there.
• Synonyms: ḥāḵām, “wise” (H2450); yāḏaʿ, “know” (H3045); śāḵal, “have insight, act wisely” (H7919)
• Antonym: kᵉsîl, “fool” (H3684)

• 1 Kings 3:9: Solomon asks for an understanding mind to discern between good and evil
• 1 Kings 3:12: God gives him a wise and discerning mind, the same pair used of Joseph
• Psalm 19:12: “Who can discern his errors?” Our own faults are the hardest thing to see
• Psalm 139:2: God discerns our thoughts from afar
• Deuteronomy 32:29: Israel failed to discern where its path was heading
Insight: Discernment starts with God, who discerns us completely, and he gives it to those who ask, as Solomon did and as Joseph acknowledged (Genesis 41:16).

• Pulpit Commentary: nāḇôn is a Niphal participle of bîn, meaning intelligent or discerning.
• Benson: Joseph wasn't angling for the job. He had just come out of prison and was urging Pharaoh to make practical use of what God had revealed.
• Barnes: Pharaoh approved the plan and chose Joseph himself as the “discreet and wise” man Joseph had described, acknowledging that his gift came from God.

Joseph's discernment came from God (Genesis 41:39), and it was practical: it saw a famine coming and turned that into a plan to store grain. Solomon's request (1 Kings 3:9) and David's prayer about hidden faults (Psalm 19:12) show the same gift turned inward as well as outward.
To consider: Where do you most need God's discernment right now, to see a situation clearly or to see something in yourself?

It's the brothers' first admission of what they did to Joseph, spoken to one another more than twenty years later (Genesis 42:21). The same verse repeats “distress” (ṣārâ, H6869) twice: Joseph's distress then, theirs now. Guilt runs through the whole week, from the brothers' consciences to Day Four's questions about conviction and condemnation.

Hebrew: אָשֵׁם (ʾāšēm), Strong's H818. In the interlinear it appears as the plural אֲשֵׁמִים (ʾăšēmîm) under “guilty,” right after אֲבָל (ʾăḇāl, “truly”).
Gloss: guilty, liable for a wrong.

Strong's defines it as guilty, and so obligated to bring a guilt offering. It comes from the verb ʾāšam (H816, to be guilty, incur guilt) and is related to the noun ʾāšām (H817, guilt, guilt offering). The word describes a real standing before God, not just a feeling: something is owed and has to be dealt with.
• Synonyms: ʿāwōn, “iniquity, guilt” (H5771); ḥāṭāʾ, “to sin” (H2398), the verb behind Judah's “bear the blame” in Genesis 43:9
• Antonyms: nāqî, “innocent” (H5355); ṣaddîq, “righteous” (H6662)

H818 appears only three times, so include its root family:
• 2 Samuel 14:13: the woman of Tekoa tells David he is acting guilty by not bringing his banished son home
• Ezra 10:19: men who had sinned offer a ram for their guilt
• Hosea 5:15 (verb, H816): God waits until his people acknowledge their guilt and seek his face
• Isaiah 53:10 (noun, H817): the Servant makes his soul an offering for guilt
• Psalm 34:22 (verb, H816): none who take refuge in the Lord will be condemned
Insight: Guilt is real and must be answered, and God provides the answer himself: an offering for guilt that ends in “no condemnation” (Romans 8:1).

• Ellicott: the brothers were suffering unjustly this time, yet their minds went straight to their old sin. That it was still so fresh is a sign real repentance was beginning.
• Matthew Henry: when the sin was new they sat down to eat; years later, trouble woke their conscience. Affliction often brings sin back to memory.
• Cambridge Bible: “distress” is used for Joseph's agony in the pit and for their present trouble, distress for distress, and Joseph's treatment was working (Hosea 5:15).

The brothers' guilt was real, and it took years and a crisis to surface. Their honest “we are guilty” was the beginning of their restoration, and Joseph wept when he heard it (Genesis 42:24). Real guilt names something specific and leads toward God, unlike the vague accusing voice Day Four called condemnation.
To consider: Is there something specific God keeps bringing to mind that needs to be confessed, or something already confessed that you need to stop carrying (Romans 8:1)?

Judah uses it twice: when he persuades Jacob to let Benjamin go (Genesis 43:9) and when he pleads with Joseph to keep him instead of Benjamin (Genesis 44:32). It's a guarantor's word, someone who stands liable for another person, and it carries Judah's whole change: the brother who sold Joseph now puts himself up as security for Rachel's other son.

Hebrew: עָרַב (ʿārab), Strong's H6148. In Genesis 43:9 the interlinear shows אֶעֶרְבֶנּוּ (ʾeʿerbennû), “I myself will guarantee him”; in Genesis 44:32 it is עָרַב (ʿārab), “guaranteed.”
Gloss: to pledge, become surety, guarantee.

Strong's gives two strands: (1) to pledge, give security, stand as guarantor, mortgage, or exchange in trade; and (2) to mix or intermingle, including to associate with or share in. The common thread is becoming bound up with someone else's fate. Brown-Driver-Briggs places Genesis 43:9 under going surety for a person's safety.
• Related: ʿērāḇôn, “pledge” (H6162), from the same root, the pledge Judah handed Tamar (Genesis 38:17–18)
• Synonym: “strike hands,” the gesture of sealing a guarantee (Proverbs 6:1; 17:18)
• Opposite: washing your hands of someone, as the brothers did with Joseph (Genesis 37:26–27)

• Proverbs 6:1: a warning about putting up security for a neighbor, since you become liable for his debt
• Nehemiah 5:3: in a famine, people mortgage their fields to get grain
• Job 17:3: Job asks who will put up security for him, and looks to God
• Psalm 119:122: the psalmist asks God himself to be his pledge of good
• Isaiah 38:14: Hezekiah, near death, prays, “be my pledge of safety!”
Insight: Proverbs treats standing surety as costly and risky, which is what makes Judah's offer remarkable, and the psalms and prophets look to God as the guarantor no one else can be (Hebrews 7:22).

• Ellicott: Judah's offer was more persuasive than Reuben's pledge of his sons' lives (Genesis 42:37) because it was real; he would stand guilty before his father the rest of his life.
• Benson: Judah's conscience had recently struck him over Joseph, and taking responsibility for Benjamin was evidence his repentance was genuine, a kind of restitution.
• Matthew Henry (on 44:18–34): Christ came from Judah (Hebrews 7:14), and he not only intercedes for transgressors but becomes their surety.

Judah went from selling a brother for silver (Genesis 37:26–27) to offering himself as a slave so that brother's full brother could go home (Genesis 44:33). A surety stands in someone else's place and takes the cost, which is the shape of what Christ has done for us (Hebrews 7:22).
To consider: Who in your life needs you to stand with them at some cost to yourself, rather than at a safe distance?

days.summary: Joseph reveals himself to his brothers and tells them God sent him ahead to save lives.

questions.text: Read Genesis 45. What was the brothers' initial response upon learning that Joseph was their brother?
questions.answer: They couldn’t answer him, because they were “dismayed at his presence” (v. 3). The powerful man who held their lives in his hands turned out to be the brother they had sold, so shock and fear came before any relief. Only after Joseph wept over them and kissed each one did they finally talk with him (v. 15).

questions.text: What do you observe about the way Joseph treated them?
questions.answer: Gently and generously. He sent the Egyptians out so the moment was private (v. 1), wept openly, and asked them to come close (v. 4). He told them not to be distressed or angry with themselves (v. 5), offered them land in Goshen and food for the rest of the famine (vv. 10–11), embraced Benjamin and kissed them all (vv. 14–15), and sent them off loaded with gifts. He even told them, “Do not quarrel on the way” (v. 24), knowing they might start blaming each other.

questions.text: What specific things did Joseph say God had done?
questions.answer:
• Sent him ahead “to preserve life” (v. 5)
• Sent him to preserve a remnant and keep many survivors alive (v. 7)
• Was the one who really sent him, not the brothers (v. 8)
• Made him a father to Pharaoh, lord of his house, and ruler over all Egypt (v. 8)
• Made him “lord of all Egypt” (v. 9)

questions.text: What did Joseph understand about God based on his life's experiences?
questions.answer: That God rules over everything, including the wrongs people do to each other. His brothers meant harm, yet God used it to keep the family alive and protect the line he had promised to Abraham (vv. 5–8). Joseph had come to read his years as a slave and prisoner through God’s purposes, and that is what freed him to forgive. He says the same thing again in Genesis 50:20.

questions.text: How did Pharaoh respond when he heard Joseph's family had come?
questions.answer: He was pleased, and so were his servants (v. 16). He told Joseph to bring his father and their households, promised them the best of the land of Egypt so they would “eat the fat of the land” (v. 18), sent wagons for the wives and little ones, and told them not to worry about belongings left behind (vv. 19–20).

questions.text: In how many ways were the descendants of Israel recipients of God's grace?
questions.answer:
• Their lives were saved from a famine with five years still to run (vv. 6–7, 11)
• They were forgiven instead of punished for selling Joseph (vv. 5, 15)
• They were offered land in Goshen, close to Joseph (v. 10)
• Joseph promised to provide for them (v. 11)
• Pharaoh gave them the best of Egypt (v. 18)
• Wagons were sent so the old and young could travel (v. 19)
• They were told not to worry about their goods (v. 20)
• Gifts of food, clothing, and silver (vv. 21–23)
• Jacob’s spirit revived when he heard Joseph was alive (v. 27)
The brothers had done nothing to earn any of it.

questions.text: As you go through your week, take note of all the specific times you are a recipient of God's grace: for example, when you receive mercy instead of judgment, forgiveness instead of criticism, when you are given material or spiritual blessings that you didn't earn and don't deserve. What do you notice?
questions.answer:
Grace is easy to miss because it often looks ordinary: a patient answer when you expected irritation, a friend who lets something go, a need met before you asked. Joseph’s brothers received grace they could never repay, and they still struggled to take it in.
To consider: Which is harder for you to receive, being forgiven or being given something you didn’t earn?

quiz.q: When Joseph said "I am Joseph," how did his brothers first react?
choices: They couldn't answer him, dismayed at his presence
quiz.why: His brothers couldn't answer him because they were dismayed at his presence (Genesis 45:3).

quiz.q: Joseph told his brothers God sent him ahead of them for what purpose?
choices: To punish them for what they did
To rule over his father's house
To learn the wisdom of Egypt
quiz.why: Joseph told them not to be distressed, because God sent him ahead to preserve life (Genesis 45:5).

quiz.q: How many more years of famine were still ahead when Joseph revealed himself?
quiz.why: The famine had lasted two years, with five more years still to come (Genesis 45:6).

quiz.q: True or false: Pharaoh was displeased when he heard Joseph's brothers had come.
quiz.why: The news pleased Pharaoh and his servants, and he invited the whole family to Egypt (Genesis 45:16-18).

quiz.q: What finally revived Jacob's spirit after he heard Joseph was alive?
choices: Seeing the wagons Joseph had sent
A dream from God that night
quiz.why: Jacob didn't believe them at first, but when he saw the wagons Joseph sent, his spirit revived (Genesis 45:26-27).

quiz.q: Joseph told his brothers that, in the end, who really sent him to Egypt?
quiz.why: Joseph said it was not his brothers who sent him there, but God (Genesis 45:8).

quiz.q: Why did Joseph tell his brothers, "Do not quarrel on the way"?
choices: He knew they might start blaming each other
He feared robbers would hear them
Benjamin was too young for arguing
quiz.why: Joseph sent them off with gifts and told them not to quarrel, knowing they might blame each other (Genesis 45:24).

quiz.q: What freed Joseph to forgive the brothers who had sold him?
choices: Time had made him forget the wrong
Pharaoh ordered him to make peace
Seeing his hard years through God's purposes
His brothers paid back what they owed
quiz.why: Joseph saw that God used his brothers' harm to keep the family alive, and that freed him to forgive (Genesis 45:5-8).

quiz.q: True or false: Joseph's brothers had done something to earn the kindness they received in Genesis 45.
quiz.why: The brothers earned none of it; they were forgiven instead of punished for selling Joseph (Genesis 45:15).

days.summary: Jacob takes the whole family to Egypt on God's promise, sees Joseph again, and settles in Goshen.

questions.text: Read Genesis 46:1-27. Compare Genesis 26:2 with Genesis 46:3. What does this show us about God's guidance in our lives?
questions.answer: In a famine, God told Isaac not to go down to Egypt but to stay in the land (Genesis 26:2). In another famine he told Jacob the opposite: “Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt” (46:3). Same place, different instructions, because God’s guidance fits the person and the moment in his larger plan. Jacob stopped at Beersheba to worship before leaving the land (46:1), and God answered with a promise to go with him (46:4). Yesterday’s direction doesn’t replace asking God today.

questions.text: How does the Holy Spirit want you to respond to this understanding?
questions.answer:
If God’s direction can change from one season to the next, a decision is worth bringing to him even when it looks like one you’ve faced before. Jacob was old and the path seemed obvious, but he still stopped to worship and listen before he moved.
To consider: What decision in front of you have you been treating as already settled without asking God about it?

questions.text: Why was Moses so careful to record all these names here?
questions.answer: The list shows the promise to Abraham taking shape: these seventy people are the beginning of the nation God said would come from him (46:27). The names also fix each family’s place for later, since Israel’s tribes and their land inheritance trace back to these sons and grandsons (compare Numbers 26). And it shows the whole household went, so the entire family of promise was now under God’s care in Egypt.

questions.text: How large was the community of Israelites living in Egypt 215 years after God first appeared to Abraham? See Exodus 12:37. How large was the community that was liberated from slavery by Moses? Connect this with Genesis 46:3-4.
questions.answer: When Jacob’s family went down to Egypt, about 215 years after God first appeared to Abraham, the whole household numbered seventy (46:27). At the exodus, Israel left with “about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides women and children” (Exodus 12:37), so the full number with families was far larger. That is God keeping his word in Genesis 46:3: “I will make you into a great nation.” He kept the next promise too: “I will also bring you up again” (46:4).

questions.text: Read Genesis 46:28-47:31. How did Joseph demonstrate wisdom in preparing for his father's move to Egypt?
questions.answer: He went to Goshen himself to meet his father (46:29). Then he planned how to present the family: he would tell Pharaoh they were shepherds, and he coached his brothers to say the same, because “every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians” (46:34). That honesty got them settled in Goshen, apart from Egyptian society. He spoke to Pharaoh first, then brought in five brothers, then Jacob (47:1–2, 7), and he provided food for every household (47:12).

questions.text: Why were the Israelites allowed to settle in their own community? How do you see God's hand in this?
questions.answer: Egyptians looked down on shepherds (46:34), so a shepherd family in its own district suited everyone, and Pharaoh gave them Goshen, “the best of the land” (47:6). God’s hand shows in the result. In Canaan the family was already blending in with the locals (Judah in chapter 38). In Goshen they had good pasture, room to grow, and enough distance from Egyptian life to stay a distinct people, and they multiplied greatly (47:27).

questions.text: How is Goshen described by Pharaoh? See Psalm 16:5-6. In what sense is this true of your own life?
questions.answer:
Pharaoh calls Goshen “the best of the land” (Genesis 47:6, 11). Psalm 16:5–6 says the Lord is the psalmist’s portion and “the lines have fallen for me in pleasant places.” The psalm’s point is that God himself is the inheritance, whatever the address.
To consider: Which “pleasant places” in your life right now have you started treating as ordinary?

questions.text: How did Joseph's family reap the benefits of his faithfulness to God? What does this say to you about your own responsibilities and the prospects of reward?
questions.answer:
Because Joseph stayed faithful as a slave, a prisoner, and a ruler, his whole family was fed through the famine, settled in the best land in Egypt, and offered work over Pharaoh’s livestock (47:6, 11–12). They benefited from years of obedience they never saw. Faithfulness usually reaches more people than the one practicing it, though Joseph suffered unfairly for a long time before any of this showed.
To consider: Who might be affected, years from now, by how faithfully you handle what’s in front of you this week?

quiz.q: Where did Jacob stop to offer sacrifices on his way to Egypt?
quiz.why: Israel came to Beersheba and offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac (Genesis 46:1).

quiz.q: During an earlier famine, what did God tell Isaac in Genesis 26:2?
choices: Go down to Egypt, and I will go with you
Do not go down to Egypt; stay in the land
Return to your family in Paddan-aram
Send your sons to buy grain in Egypt
quiz.why: God told Isaac not to go down to Egypt but to live in the land he would show him (Genesis 26:2), the opposite of his word to Jacob (Genesis 46:3).

quiz.q: How many people of Jacob's house came into Egypt in all?
quiz.why: All the persons of the house of Jacob who came into Egypt were seventy (Genesis 46:27).

quiz.q: True or false: Egyptians considered every shepherd an abomination.
quiz.why: Joseph coached his brothers to say they kept livestock so they could live in Goshen, since every shepherd was an abomination to the Egyptians (Genesis 46:34).

quiz.q: How old did Jacob tell Pharaoh he was?
quiz.why: Jacob told Pharaoh the years of his sojourning were 130 (Genesis 47:9).

quiz.q: Why did God tell Isaac and Jacob opposite things about going down to Egypt?
choices: He had changed his mind about the promise
Jacob had more faith than Isaac
His guidance fits the person and the moment in his plan
Egypt had become a safer place
quiz.why: God's guidance fits the person and the moment, so he told Jacob, "Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt" (Genesis 46:3).

quiz.q: What does the careful list of seventy names in Genesis 46 show?
choices: The beginning of the nation God promised Abraham
Who would serve in Pharaoh's court
The family members who stayed in Canaan
quiz.why: The seventy who went to Egypt were the start of the nation God promised would come from Abraham (Genesis 46:27).

quiz.q: About how many men on foot left Egypt at the exodus, besides women and children?
quiz.why: Seventy went down, and about six hundred thousand men left, as God promised to make them a great nation (Exodus 12:37).

quiz.q: True or false: Living apart in Goshen helped Jacob's family stay a distinct people instead of blending in.
quiz.why: Set apart in Goshen with good pasture, Israel stayed distinct and multiplied greatly (Genesis 47:27).

days.summary: Joseph manages the famine, Israel grows, and Jacob blesses Joseph's sons, crossing his hands to put the younger first.

questions.text: What impact did Joseph have on Egyptian society?
questions.answer: He reshaped Egypt’s economy. As the famine went on, people paid for grain first with money, then livestock, then their land and themselves, until nearly all the land belonged to Pharaoh (47:14–20). Only the priests kept theirs (v. 22). He handed out seed and set a lasting rule that a fifth of every harvest went to Pharaoh (vv. 23–26). Verse 21 says either that he made the people servants or that he moved them into the cities, depending on the manuscript; the ESV has the first, with the second in a footnote.

questions.text: How do you view his handling of the problems the famine brought? How did the Egyptian people see him?
questions.answer: Readers differ here. Many see Joseph as a wise administrator who kept a nation alive and set a tax of one fifth, which is often described as moderate for the ancient world. Others are uneasy that he used the crisis to put land and people under Pharaoh, which foreshadows Israel’s own slavery later. The Egyptians themselves were grateful: “You have saved our lives” (v. 25).

questions.text: Despite the crisis the famine brought to the whole region, what was happening to the family of Israel during this time according to Genesis 47:27? What encouragement can you take from this?
questions.answer:
While Egypt and Canaan were wasting away, Israel settled in Goshen, gained possessions, and “were fruitful and multiplied greatly” (47:27). God’s people grew in the middle of a crisis that was emptying everyone else’s storehouses. A hard season doesn’t pause what God is doing among his people.
To consider: What hard season are you in where growth might be happening quietly?

questions.text: What reference does Hebrews 11:21 make to Jacob's attitude as his life began to draw to a close?
questions.answer: It says that “by faith” Jacob, when dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons and worshipped, “bowing in worship over the head of his staff” (Hebrews 11:21). At the end, his posture was trust and worship, not regret. The staff detail follows the Greek translation of Genesis 47:31, where the Hebrew reads “bed.”

questions.text: What specific things do you think he may have thought about as he reflected back on his life and worshipped God?
questions.answer:
Genesis 48 gives hints in his own words:
• God appearing to him at Luz (Bethel) and promising land and descendants (48:3–4)
• Rachel’s death on the road to Bethlehem (48:7)
• Thinking he would never see Joseph again, and now holding Joseph’s sons (48:11)
• God shepherding him his whole life (48:15)
• The angel who redeemed him from all evil (48:16), perhaps recalling his wrestling at Peniel (32:24–30)
He may also have remembered his own deceptions and how God stayed with him anyway.

questions.text: Spend some time reflecting on God's blessings in your life and worshipping him. Does any particular song help you to connect with God today in that way?
questions.answer:
Jacob worshipped at the end of a life that held real grief, so worship doesn’t have to wait until everything is tidy. A song can carry you when your own words run dry.
To consider: Which song puts words to God’s faithfulness in your story, and which line of it do you need most today?

questions.text: Read Genesis 48. Why did Jacob "adopt" the sons of Joseph?
questions.answer: He claimed Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons, ranking them with Reuben and Simeon (48:5). That gave Joseph a double share, since each boy would become a tribe with its own inheritance. In effect the firstborn’s double portion went to Joseph, Rachel’s firstborn, after Reuben lost it (1 Chronicles 5:1–2). It also tied two half-Egyptian boys firmly to God’s promise of the land (48:4).

questions.text: Which of Joseph's sons received the greater blessing? How many other times in Genesis do you remember that kind of reversal?
questions.answer:
Ephraim, the younger. Jacob crossed his hands to put his right hand on Ephraim’s head and refused when Joseph tried to correct him (48:14, 17–19). Other times Genesis favors the younger:
• Abel’s offering accepted over Cain’s (4:4–5)
• Isaac chosen over Ishmael (17:19–21; 21:12)
• Jacob over Esau (25:23; ch. 27)
• Rachel loved more than Leah (29:30)
• Perez breaking out ahead of Zerah (38:27–30)
• Joseph raised above his older brothers (37:5–11)

questions.text: Which name for God does Jacob use in Genesis 48:3? What does this name mean in Hebrew? What does this name mean to you?
questions.answer:
“God Almighty,” in Hebrew El Shaddai (48:3). El means God. The origin of Shaddai is debated: it has been linked to might or overpowering, to a word for mountain, and sometimes to the word for breast, suggesting the God who nourishes and is enough. In Genesis the name comes with promises of fruitfulness made when they looked impossible (17:1; 35:11).
To consider: Where do you need God to be almighty for you right now, not just in theory?

quiz.q: When the Egyptians' money ran out, what did they give Joseph next for food?
quiz.why: When the money was gone, Joseph gave them food in exchange for their horses, flocks, herds, and donkeys (Genesis 47:15-17).

quiz.q: What share of the harvest did Joseph require the people to give Pharaoh?
quiz.why: Joseph gave the people seed and told them to give a fifth of each harvest to Pharaoh (Genesis 47:24, 26).

quiz.q: According to Hebrews 11:21, what did Jacob do by faith as he was dying?
choices: Blessed each of Joseph's sons and worshipped
quiz.why: By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of Joseph's sons and worshipped, leaning on his staff (Hebrews 11:21).

quiz.q: True or false: Jacob put his right hand on the head of Manasseh, the firstborn.
quiz.why: Jacob crossed his hands and put his right hand on Ephraim, the younger, and his left on Manasseh (Genesis 48:14).

quiz.q: Which name for God did Jacob use in Genesis 48:3?
quiz.why: Jacob told Joseph that God Almighty (El Shaddai) appeared to him at Luz and blessed him (Genesis 48:3).

quiz.q: True or false: Egypt's priests also had to sell their land to Pharaoh during the famine.
quiz.why: Nearly all the land went to Pharaoh, but the priests kept theirs (Genesis 47:22).

quiz.q: Why did Jacob claim Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons?
choices: Joseph asked him to raise them in Canaan
To replace Benjamin as his youngest
To give Joseph a double share of the inheritance
Pharaoh required it before Jacob died
quiz.why: Ranking the boys with Reuben and Simeon gave Joseph the firstborn's double portion, two tribes (Genesis 48:5).

quiz.q: Which is another time Genesis favors a younger one over the older?
quiz.why: Like Ephraim over Manasseh, God chose Jacob over his older brother Esau (Genesis 25:23).

quiz.q: In Genesis, the name El Shaddai often comes with what kind of promise?
quiz.why: God Almighty, El Shaddai, made promises of fruitfulness when they looked impossible (Genesis 35:11).

days.summary: Jacob's blessing calls God his shepherd all his life long. Psalm 23 and Jesus the Good Shepherd.

questions.text: In Genesis 48:15-16, list the ways in which Jacob described God.
questions.answer:
• The God before whom his fathers Abraham and Isaac walked (v. 15)
• The God who has been his shepherd all his life long to this day (v. 15)
• The angel who redeemed him from all evil (v. 16)
Many Christians read this angel as God himself appearing, possibly the pre-incarnate Christ (compare 32:30); others take it as God’s messenger acting on his behalf.

questions.text: Have you known God as "the God before whom your fathers walked"?
questions.answer:
Jacob knew God first as the God of his grandfather and father, and only later as his own. Many people meet God through someone else’s faith before it becomes personal.
To consider: Whose walk with God shaped how you first knew him, and what would you want someone after you to say about yours?

questions.text: What does Psalm 23 tell us we will receive if God is our shepherd?
questions.answer:
• Lack nothing (v. 1)
• Rest in green pastures and beside still waters (v. 2)
• A restored soul (v. 3)
• Guidance in paths of righteousness for his name’s sake (v. 3)
• No need to fear evil in “the valley of the shadow of death,” because he is with us (v. 4)
• Comfort from his rod and staff (v. 4)
• A table prepared in the presence of enemies (v. 5)
• An anointed head and an overflowing cup (v. 5)
• Goodness and mercy following us all our days (v. 6)
• A home in the house of the Lord forever (v. 6)

questions.text: In what ways does Jesus, our good shepherd, care for his sheep as described in John 10:1-18?
questions.answer:
• He calls his own sheep by name (v. 3)
• He leads them out and goes ahead of them (vv. 3–4)
• His sheep know his voice and follow him (vv. 4, 14)
• He is the door; whoever enters by him is saved and finds pasture (v. 9)
• He came so they may have life “and have it abundantly” (v. 10)
• He lays down his life for the sheep (vv. 11, 15)
• He doesn’t run from danger like the hired hand (vv. 12–13)
• He knows his own and they know him (v. 14)
• He brings other sheep too, into one flock (v. 16)
• He lays down his life of his own accord and takes it up again (vv. 17–18)

questions.text: Have you known God as your shepherd? Can you think of specific examples?
questions.answer:
Jacob said God had shepherded him “all my life long” near the end of his life, and many of those years hadn’t felt like being led. Shepherding often shows up as provision, a closed door, or the right person arriving at the right time.
To consider: Think of one season that felt aimless while you were in it. Where can you now see God leading you through it?

questions.text: Have you known God as the one who has delivered you from all harm? Can you think of examples?
questions.answer:
Jacob spoke of the angel who “redeemed me from all evil” (48:16) as a man who had been cheated, had lost Rachel, and had mourned Joseph for years. Deliverance didn’t mean nothing bad happened to him. It meant evil didn’t get the last word.
To consider: Is there a harm you were spared, or brought through, that you’ve never specifically thanked God for?

questions.text: What promise, gift and instruction did Jacob make to Joseph as he was about to die?
questions.answer:
• Promise: God will be with Joseph and bring him back to the land of his fathers (48:21)
• Gift: one extra portion of land beyond his brothers, taken from the Amorites (48:22); the Hebrew word is shechem, likely pointing to Shechem, where Joseph’s bones were later buried (Joshua 24:32)
• Instruction: not to bury him in Egypt but with his fathers in Canaan, sworn with Joseph’s hand under his thigh (47:29–31)

quiz.q: In his blessing, Jacob said God had been his what "all my life long to this day"?
quiz.why: Jacob spoke of the God who had been his shepherd all his life long (Genesis 48:15).

quiz.q: In Psalm 23:2, where does the Lord lead the psalmist?
quiz.why: He makes me lie down in green pastures and leads me beside still waters (Psalm 23:2).

quiz.q: In John 10, what does Jesus say the good shepherd does for the sheep?
choices: Lays down his life for them
Builds a stronger fold for them
quiz.why: Jesus said, "I am the good shepherd," who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11).

quiz.q: True or false: In John 10, the hired hand stays to protect the sheep when the wolf comes.
quiz.why: The hired hand sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees, because he doesn't care for them (John 10:12-13).

quiz.q: What did Jacob make Joseph swear to do before he died?
quiz.why: Jacob had Joseph put his hand under his thigh and swear to bury him with his fathers, not in Egypt (Genesis 47:29-31).

quiz.q: Jacob called God "the angel who has" done what for him?
quiz.why: Jacob blessed the boys in the name of the angel who redeemed him from all evil (Genesis 48:16).

quiz.q: In Psalm 23:4, why need we not fear in the valley of the shadow of death?
quiz.why: We fear no evil in the valley of the shadow of death, because the shepherd is with us (Psalm 23:4).

quiz.q: In John 10, how does the good shepherd call his own sheep?
quiz.why: The good shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out (John 10:3).

quiz.q: True or false: Jacob gave Joseph one extra portion of land beyond what his brothers received.
quiz.why: Jacob gave Joseph one portion more than his brothers, likely Shechem, where Joseph's bones were later buried (Genesis 48:22).

days.summary: Jacob blesses his sons and dies. The brothers fear revenge; Joseph forgives them and looks ahead to the promised land.

questions.text: Read through Genesis 49. What strikes you? Which names seem most significant?
questions.answer:
Jacob’s words match how each son lived. Reuben loses the firstborn’s place for sleeping with Bilhah (vv. 3–4; 35:22). Simeon and Levi are scattered for their violence at Shechem (vv. 5–7; ch. 34). Judah, who once proposed selling Joseph but later offered himself for Benjamin, receives a royal promise (vv. 8–12). Joseph gets the richest blessing (vv. 22–26). Judah and Joseph stand out most. Midway, Jacob breaks off to pray, “I wait for your salvation, O Lord” (v. 18).
To consider: Which son’s words surprise you most, and why?

questions.text: Which verse in this chapter contains a messianic prophecy?
questions.answer: Verse 10: “The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet.” The next line is hard to translate; the ESV has “until tribute comes to him,” with footnotes giving “until Shiloh comes” or “until he comes to whom it belongs.” Jews and Christians have long read it as pointing to a coming king. Christians see it fulfilled in David’s line and in Jesus, “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” (Revelation 5:5).

questions.text: Read Genesis 50. What did the brothers fear when Jacob died?
questions.answer: They feared Joseph had held back only for their father’s sake. With Jacob gone, they thought he might hate them and pay them back for all the evil they had done to him (50:15).

questions.text: How did they handle this situation? What was Joseph's response?
questions.answer: They sent Joseph a message saying that Jacob, before he died, had asked him to forgive them (vv. 16–17). Genesis never records Jacob saying this, so some readers suspect they invented it. Then they came, fell down before him, and offered themselves as his servants (v. 18). Joseph wept (v. 17). He told them not to fear, asked, “Am I in the place of God?” and said God had meant their evil for good (vv. 19–20). He promised to provide for them and their children and spoke kindly to them (v. 21).

questions.text: Why didn't the brothers truly believe Joseph had forgiven them? Do we ever similarly grieve God?
questions.answer: Guilt makes forgiveness hard to accept. They knew what they deserved, and they may have expected Joseph to act like Esau, who planned to kill Jacob once their father died (27:41). Seventeen years of kindness hadn’t convinced them, and Joseph wept at being doubted (50:17). We can do the same to God when we keep confessing a forgiven sin as if he didn’t mean it, or live as though punishment is still pending (compare 1 John 1:9).

questions.text: How did Joseph demonstrate that he had completely forgiven his brothers?
questions.answer:
• He refused revenge: “Am I in the place of God?” (v. 19)
• He saw God’s good purpose in what they had done (v. 20)
• He told them twice not to be afraid (vv. 19, 21)
• He promised to provide for them and their little ones (v. 21)
• He comforted them and spoke kindly to them (v. 21)
He had already been providing for them for seventeen years (45:11; 47:12).

questions.text: Is there any sin you have committed which you have trouble believing God has forgiven you for? How do Psalm 103:3-4 and 9, combined with the story of Joseph, help you?
questions.answer:
Psalm 103 says God forgives all your iniquity and redeems your life from the pit (vv. 3–4), and that he “will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever” (v. 9). Joseph’s brothers were forgiven long before they believed it, and their fear only hurt them and grieved him. Feeling forgiven can lag far behind being forgiven.
To consider: If there’s a sin you keep bringing back to God, what would it look like this week to take him at his word that it’s settled?

questions.text: How old was Joseph when he died? What promise did he extract from his brothers?
questions.answer: Joseph died at 110 (50:22, 26). He made the sons of Israel swear that when God visited them and brought them out, they would carry his bones up from Egypt (50:25). They kept the oath: Moses took the bones at the exodus (Exodus 13:19), and they were buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32).

questions.text: What prophetic words did Joseph speak concerning the nation of Israel? How long did it take for the prophecy to be fulfilled? (Exodus 12:40)
questions.answer: Joseph said, “I am about to die, but God will visit you and bring you up out of this land” to the land he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (50:24), and repeated that God would surely visit them (v. 25). Exodus 12:40 says Israel lived in Egypt 430 years before it came true. God had told Abraham his descendants would be afflicted in a foreign land for 400 years and then come out (Genesis 15:13–14).

quiz.q: Which son did Jacob call a lion's cub, from whom the scepter would not depart?
quiz.why: Jacob called Judah a lion's cub and said the scepter would not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:9-10).

quiz.q: After Jacob died, what were Joseph's brothers afraid of?
choices: That Pharaoh would send them away
That Joseph would pay them back for their evil
That the Canaanites would attack Goshen
quiz.why: They worried Joseph would hate them and repay them for all the evil they had done to him (Genesis 50:15).

quiz.q: In Genesis 50:20, what did Joseph say God meant the brothers' evil for?
choices: For good, to keep many people alive
To teach them a hard lesson
To make Joseph rich and powerful
quiz.why: Joseph said they meant evil against him, but God meant it for good, so many people would be kept alive (Genesis 50:20).

quiz.q: True or false: Psalm 103:9 says the Lord will keep his anger forever.
quiz.why: The psalm says he will not always chide, nor keep his anger forever (Psalm 103:9).

quiz.q: How old was Joseph when he died?
quiz.why: Joseph died at 110 years old and was embalmed and put in a coffin in Egypt (Genesis 50:26).

quiz.q: Christians see Genesis 49:10 fulfilled in Jesus, called what in Revelation 5:5?
choices: The Lion of the tribe of Judah
quiz.why: The scepter promised to Judah points to Jesus, "the Lion of the tribe of Judah" (Revelation 5:5).

quiz.q: The brothers may have expected Joseph to act like whom, who planned revenge once his father died?
quiz.why: They may have feared Joseph would act like Esau, who planned to kill Jacob after their father died (Genesis 27:41).

quiz.q: Which of these did Joseph do to show he had completely forgiven his brothers?
choices: Promised to provide for them and their little ones
Made them swear loyalty to Pharaoh
Accepted their offer to be his servants
Sent them back to live in Canaan
quiz.why: Joseph told them not to fear and promised to provide for them and their little ones (Genesis 50:21).

quiz.q: True or false: Genesis records Jacob actually asking Joseph to forgive his brothers.
quiz.why: The brothers' message claimed Jacob asked this, but Genesis never records him saying it (Genesis 50:16-17).

days.summary: Four word-study options from Genesis 48–50: chashab (“meant,” 50:20), raʿah (“shepherd,” 48:15), gaʾal (“redeemed,” 48:16), and paqad (“visit,” 50:24), tracing God’s purpose, care, rescue, and faithfulness to his promise.

questions.text: From your reading this week, choose ONE WORD to research. Is there a word that is repeated? Is there a word that strikes you as especially significant or “jumps out” at you? Is there a word that intrigues or puzzles you? Your Word of the Week:

Type in your verse reference at biblehub.com. Click the Interlinear tab (“Int” on a mobile device) at the top in order to find the word in the original language. Click the link to the Strong’s number to view the Lexical Summary. What is the Hebrew word and the Strong’s #?
What are the range of meanings you find when search the Strong’s definitions? What are synonyms or antonyms?
From the column on the right, find several other places in the Old Testament where this word is used. Click on the link to read the verse. What insight does this give you?
Now, type in your verse reference again at biblehub.com, but this time click the Commentaries tab. Browse through these to see if you can gain any additional helpful information.

What has your study taught you? Have you been able to find a point of application? As you have spent time meditating on the meaning of this word in this passage, has God given you any insight into why this word stood out to you today?
Which of God’s attributes were most clear to you this week?
questions.answer:
• Sovereign over human choices: he turned the brothers’ evil plan to good (Genesis 50:20)
• Shepherd: he led and fed Jacob all his life (Genesis 48:15; Psalm 23:1)
• Forgiving and compassionate: he does not deal with us according to our sins (Psalm 103:10)
• Faithful to his promises: he would surely visit Israel and bring them to the land (Genesis 50:24)
To consider: Which of these do you find hardest to believe about God right now, and why?

questions.text: Which passages or insights were most meaningful to you this week? Explain.
questions.answer:
• Genesis 45:5-8: Joseph says three times that God sent him before he says anything about what his brothers did.
• Genesis 48:15-16: the man who told Pharaoh his days were “few and evil” (Genesis 47:9) now calls God his shepherd and redeemer all his life.
• Genesis 50:15-21: seventeen years after Joseph forgave them, the brothers still feared payback, and he wept. Forgiveness can be given and still go unreceived.
To consider: Which of these three scenes reads most like your own story this week?

questions.text: How have you applied what you’ve discovered this week about God, others, or yourself?
questions.answer:
Joseph applied what he knew about God in how he treated people who had wronged him: he “comforted them and spoke kindly to them” (Genesis 50:21). Psalm 103 asks for a parallel response toward God: receiving his forgiveness instead of waiting to be punished (Psalm 103:3, 9-10).
To consider: Who is one person you could speak kindly to this week specifically because of how God has dealt with you?

answers: Joseph uses the same verb twice in one sentence: his brothers “meant” evil against him, and God “meant” it for good (Genesis 50:20). The whole Joseph story turns on that word and on whose plan wins.

חָשַׁב (chashab), Strong’s H2803: to think, plan, devise, reckon. The interlinear shows it under both halves of Genesis 50:20, ḥă·šaḇ·tem (“you intended”) and ḥă·šā·ḇāh (“he intended it”). BibleHub’s interlinear glosses it “intended,” where the ESV has “meant.”

• Think, consider, regard, value (Isaiah 53:4)
• Count or credit to someone’s account (Genesis 15:6)
• Plan, devise, plot, often in a bad sense (Micah 2:1)
• Design skilled work as a weaver or craftsman (Exodus 35:35)
Strong’s gives the root idea as to plait or weave, then to fabricate or contrive. Synonyms: yaʿats (H3289, to counsel, plan) and zamam (H2161, to devise, purpose). The related noun machashabah (H4284) means a thought or plan. For an opposite, Psalm 32:2 negates the same verb: the Lord does not count iniquity against the forgiven.

• Genesis 15:6: God “counted” Abram’s faith as righteousness; his reckoning is a gift
• Exodus 35:35: craftsmen who “design” for the tabernacle; the word can describe careful, skilled work
• Psalm 32:2: blessed is the one whose iniquity the Lord does not count
• Micah 2:1: people who “devise” wickedness on their beds; the same skill aimed at harm
• Jeremiah 29:11: “the plans I have for you” pairs this verb with its noun
Insight: Chashab covers both skilled design and evil plotting, and in Genesis 50:20 both kinds of planning work on the same event. God’s plan is the one that holds.

• Ellicott: the Hebrew verb is the same in both halves of the verse, setting man’s purpose against God’s; Joseph had already said this in Genesis 45:7.
• Pulpit Commentary: literally, “you were thinking evil against me; God was thinking it for good,” meaning God intended the very thing they did to turn out well.
• Gill: God is not the author of their sin, yet the act fell under his purpose and he brought good from it; Gill compares the crucifixion.
Benson and Matthew Henry add that Joseph returned good for evil and spoke kindly to them (Genesis 50:21).

The brothers’ plan was real and it was evil, and Joseph never pretends otherwise. But it wasn’t the only plan at work in that pit and that sale. Because Joseph could see God’s plan, he could forgive without calling the wrong harmless.
To consider: What harm done to you are you still reading only through the other person’s intent, and what would change if you asked what God meant in it?

The word runs through the week. Jacob’s sons tell Pharaoh they are shepherds (Genesis 46:32; 47:3), a trade Egyptians despised (Genesis 46:34). Then the dying Jacob calls God “the God who has been my shepherd all my life long to this day” (Genesis 48:15), the first place Scripture pictures God as a shepherd. Psalm 23 and John 10 build on it.

רָעָה (raʿah), Strong’s H7462: to shepherd, tend, pasture, feed. In Genesis 48:15 it is a participle, hā·rō·ʿeh, “who has been shepherd,” meaning the one shepherding me. Psalm 23:1 uses the same word: “The LORD is my shepherd” (rō·ʿî).

Strong’s: to tend a flock, to graze, to rule, and by extension to keep company with as a friend. KJV renders it feed, keep sheep, shepherd, pastor, herdman, companion. Brown-Driver-Briggs: pasture, tend, graze. The Topical Lexicon notes it covers feeding, guiding, protecting, and seeking the lost, and that Israel’s kings were called to “shepherd” the people (2 Samuel 5:2). Synonym: nahal (H5095), to lead to rest (Psalm 23:2). Opposite: puts (H6327), to scatter (Jeremiah 23:2). Don’t confuse it with raʿah, “evil” (H7451), spelled with the same letters in Genesis 50:20.

• Genesis 37:2: seventeen-year-old Joseph “was pasturing the flock with his brothers”
• Genesis 49:24: Jacob calls God “the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel” in Joseph’s blessing
• Psalm 80:1: “O Shepherd of Israel, you who lead Joseph like a flock”
• Isaiah 40:11: he tends his flock and gathers the lambs in his arms
• Ezekiel 34:23: God promises one shepherd, “my servant David,” to feed his people
Insight: The word starts as the family trade and becomes Jacob’s name for God. The prophets then point it toward a coming shepherd-king, which Jesus claims in John 10.

• Ellicott: Jacob names God three ways in verses 15–16: the God his fathers walked before, the God who as a shepherd watched over him all his life, and the redeeming Angel.
• Keil & Delitzsch: “fed me” means led and provided for with a shepherd’s faithfulness, and they point to Psalm 23:1.
• MacLaren: Jacob told Pharaoh his days were “few and evil” (Genesis 47:9), but on his deathbed he saw them as one long shepherding by God. The difference is whether God is in the picture.

Jacob spent his working life with sheep, so he knew what a shepherd does on ordinary days: finding water and grass, moving the flock, staying with the weak ones. Looking back, he saw God had done that for him every day, including the years he had called “few and evil” (Genesis 47:9).
To consider: If you summed up your life the way Jacob did in Genesis 48:15, which season would you have to reread?

Jacob calls God “the angel who has redeemed me from all evil” (Genesis 48:16). This is the first time gaʾal appears in the Bible, and it returns in this week’s Psalm: “who redeems your life from the pit” (Psalm 103:4).

גָּאַל (gaʾal), Strong’s H1350: to redeem, act as kinsman-redeemer, avenge, ransom. In Genesis 48:16 it is the participle hag·gō·ʾêl, “who has redeemed,” the same form Psalm 103:4 uses (hag·gō·w·ʾêl).

Strong’s: to redeem according to the law of kinship; to be the next of kin and buy back a relative’s property or marry his widow; in justice, to act as avenger. KJV: redeem, redeemer, kinsman, deliver, ransom, purchase, avenger. The participle gōʾēl is the kinsman-redeemer (Ruth 3:12). Synonym: padah (H6299), to ransom or rescue. Opposite: makar (H4376), to sell, the word Joseph uses for “you sold me” (Genesis 45:5). Leviticus 25:25 puts the two together: a poor brother sells, and his nearest redeemer buys it back.

• Exodus 6:6: “I will redeem you with an outstretched arm,” God’s promise to bring Israel out of Egypt
• Leviticus 25:25: the nearest relative buys back what a poor brother has sold
• Ruth 4:4: Boaz offers the closer relative the right to redeem the family land
• Job 19:25: “I know that my Redeemer lives”
• Isaiah 43:1: “Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name”
Insight: A redeemer is family who pays to get you back. Jacob was saying God had acted as his next of kin, and Exodus 6:6 shows God doing the same for the whole family Jacob brought to Egypt.

• Cambridge Bible: to redeem is to play the kinsman’s part (Leviticus 25:48-49; Ruth 3:13). Here the rescue is from calamity, and “the angel” is indistinguishable from the God of Jacob, likely the one he met at Peniel (Genesis 32:30).
• Benson (also Gill and Poole): this is no created angel but Christ, since he redeems from all evil and Jacob prays to him for the blessing.
• Matthew Henry: Jacob knew plenty of hardship, but God kept him from the evil of his troubles.
Ellicott, on the verse 15 page, notes this is the word’s first use in Scripture.

Jacob was not spared trouble. He was cheated by Laban, buried Rachel on the road, and mourned Joseph for years. He still called God the relative who stepped in and bought him back, and Psalm 103:4 makes the same claim for everyone who belongs to God.
To consider: Where are you still trying to buy yourself back from a failure or loss that God has already paid to redeem?

words.gloss: to visit, attend to, take note of, appoint
answers: Joseph’s last words use this verb four times in two verses: “God will surely visit you” (Genesis 50:24-25). Translations puzzle over it (ESV “visit,” NIV “come to your aid,” NASB “take care of you”), and Moses quotes the phrase when he carries out Joseph’s bones (Exodus 13:19).

פָּקַד (paqad), Strong’s H6485: to visit, attend to, take note of, appoint, muster. The interlinear shows it twice in a row in Genesis 50:24, pā·qōḏ yip̄·qōḏ, literally “attending, he will attend.” Doubling a verb this way is how Hebrew says “surely.”

Strong’s: to visit, with friendly or hostile intent, and by extension to oversee, muster, take charge of, care for, miss, or deposit. KJV renders it visit, appoint, number, punish, remember, oversee, and more. Brown-Driver-Briggs gives the basic sense as “attend to, pay attention to.” It appears 302 times. God’s visit can bring help (Genesis 21:1) or judgment (Exodus 34:7). Synonym: zakar (H2142), to remember (Genesis 30:22). Opposite: shakach (H7911), to forget (Psalm 103:2).

• Genesis 21:1: the Lord “visited” Sarah as he had said, and she bore Isaac
• Exodus 3:16: God tells Moses, “I have observed you,” with the same doubled verb Joseph used
• Exodus 4:31: the people heard that the Lord had “visited” Israel, believed, and worshiped
• Exodus 13:19: Moses takes Joseph’s bones, quoting his oath word for word
• Jeremiah 23:2: the shepherds did not “attend to” the flock, so God will “attend to” them for their evil
Insight: When God visits, he comes to act on what he has said, in rescue or in reckoning. Joseph’s phrase came back generations later as the sign that the exodus had begun.

• Pulpit Commentary: literally “visiting he will visit you,” in line with God’s promise to Jacob in Genesis 46:4; Hebrews 11:22 counts this as Joseph’s act of faith.
• Ellicott: these words show Joseph’s faith and prepare for the book of Exodus, tying the two books together.
• Matthew Henry: leaving his bones unburied kept Israel expecting to leave Egypt and kept Canaan in their minds.
Keil & Delitzsch add that the coffin stayed in Egypt until the exodus and was buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32).

Joseph died with the promise still unkept and staked his burial on it. Every Israelite who passed his coffin in Egypt had a reminder that God would come. Paqad says God pays attention and shows up to act, even when the wait runs past a lifetime.
To consider: What promise of God are you waiting on, and what reminder could you keep in front of you that he will come?
